Final Conceptual Answer: \(\mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Fe} > \mathrm{Cu}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q07 - Increasing charge required for electrochemical transformations

questiontext.text:
Consider the following stoichiometric electrochemical transformations:

(I) Complete oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)
(II) Complete oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) to \(\mathrm{O}_2\)
(III) Complete reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) to metallic \(\mathrm{Al}\)
(IV) Complete reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) in acidic solution
(V) Complete reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\) to \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) in acidic solution

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these processes arranged in order of increasing quantity of electric charge (in Faradays) consumed per mole of the specified starting reactant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Relationship (Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis)
According to Faraday's laws of electrolysis, the total electric charge \(Q\) required to transform \(1\text{ mol}\) of a substance is directly proportional to the number of moles of electrons \(n\) exchanged in the balanced half-reaction:
\[Q = n \cdot F\] where \(F \approx 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\) is the Faraday constant. Hence, the required charge in Faradays equals the stoichiometric electron exchange coefficient \(n\).

Step 2: Analysis and Stoichiometric Calculation for Each Transformation
\(\bullet\) Transformation (I): In \(\mathrm{FeO}\), the oxidation state of iron is \(+2\). In \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\), the oxidation state of iron is \(+3\). The balanced half-reaction per mole of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) is:
\[\mathrm{FeO} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 + \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{e}^-\]
Here, \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrons is transferred per mole of \(\mathrm{FeO}\). Therefore, \(Q_1 = 1\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (II): In \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\), whereas in \(\mathrm{O}_2\) it is \(0\). The balanced half-reaction per mole of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) is:
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}^+ + 2\mathrm{e}^-\]
Here, \(2\text{ mol}\) of electrons are released per mole of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\). Therefore, \(Q_2 = 2\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (III): The reduction of aluminium ion to metallic aluminium follows:
\[\mathrm{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}\]
Here, \(3\text{ mol}\) of electrons are required per mole of \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\). Therefore, \(Q_3 = 3\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (IV): In permanganate (\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\), manganese has an oxidation state of \(+7\), and is reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (\(+2\)) in acidic solution:
\[\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 8\mathrm{H}^+ + 5\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Here, \(5\text{ mol}\) of electrons are consumed per mole of \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\). Therefore, \(Q_4 = 5\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (V): In dichromate (\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\)), each chromium atom is in the \(+6\) oxidation state. The reduction of one mole of dichromate ions to \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) requires:
\[\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-} + 14\mathrm{H}^+ + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} + 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Here, \(6\text{ mol}\) of electrons are consumed per mole of \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\). Therefore, \(Q_5 = 6\text{ F}\).

Step 3: Determination of the Increasing Sequence
Comparing the charge values in units of Faradays:
\(1\text{ F} < 2\text{ F} < 3\text{ F} < 5\text{ F} < 6\text{ F}\)
Matching the respective Roman numeral labels gives:
(I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The stoichiometric requirement of electrons per mole of reactant increases strictly in the sequence of \(1\text{ F} \rightarrow 2\text{ F} \rightarrow 3\text{ F} \rightarrow 5\text{ F} \rightarrow 6\text{ F}\), establishing that the increasing sequence is (I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q08 - Sequence of processes in lead-acid battery discharge and recharge

questiontext.text:
Consider the complete operational cycle consisting of the discharge and subsequent recharging of a secondary lead storage battery. Examine the following chemical and physical events:

(I) Spontaneous oxidation of lead anode to \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s})\) and simultaneous reduction of \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\) cathode to \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s})\), consuming \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).
(II) Progressive decrease in electrolyte density below \(1.20\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), signaling depletion of sulfuric acid.
(III) Application of an external electrical potential greater than cell potential with current driven in the reverse direction.
(IV) Electrolytic conversion of \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s})\) deposits back into spongy \(\mathrm{Pb}\) at the negative plate and \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\) at the positive plate, restoring sulfuric acid concentration.

Which of the following presents the correct chronological sequence of these events throughout the complete discharge and recharge cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrochemistry of the Lead Storage Battery
A lead storage battery functions as a galvanic cell during discharge and as an electrolytic cell during recharging.

Step 2: Analysis of the Full Operational Sequence
\(\bullet\) During spontaneous discharge (galvanic action), lead at the anode is oxidized: \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), while lead dioxide at the cathode is reduced: \(\mathrm{PbO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 4\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)}\). Both electrodes become coated with insoluble lead sulfate, and sulfuric acid is consumed. This corresponds to event (I).
\(\bullet\) As sulfuric acid (\(\text{density} \approx 1.30\text{ g cm}^{-3}\)) is continuously consumed to produce water (\(\text{density} \approx 1.00\text{ g cm}^{-3}\)), the density of the electrolyte drops progressively. When the density decreases below approximately \(1.20\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), the cell is substantially discharged and requires recharging. This corresponds to event (II).
\(\bullet\) To recharge the battery, it must be connected to an external direct-current power supply possessing a voltage greater than the battery's terminal voltage, thereby forcing electrons in the reverse direction into the cell. This corresponds to event (III).
\(\bullet\) Under this driven electrolytic regime, the electrode processes are reversed: \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4\) on the negative plates is reduced back to spongy metallic lead: \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq})\), while \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4\) on the positive plates is oxidized back to lead dioxide: \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 4\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), which regenerates \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) and restores the original electrolyte density. This corresponds to event (IV).

Step 3: Chronological Assembly
The natural chronological sequence encompassing discharge, exhaustion, external power connection, and regeneration is: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Discharge reactions produce lead sulfate and dilute the acid; this causes the density to drop; subsequently, an external charging potential is applied, driving the reverse electrolytic reactions that regenerate lead, lead dioxide, and concentrated sulfuric acid. The sequence is strictly (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Opposing external potential in Daniell cell

questiontext.text: In a standard Daniell cell operating at \(298\text{ K}\) with \([\text{Zn}^{2+}] = [\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\), an external opposing potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is applied across the cell. When the opposing potential reaches exactly \(1.1\text{ V}\), what is observed regarding the current and chemical reaction in the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A standard Daniell cell has an electromotive force of \(1.1\text{ V}\). When an external opposing potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is applied against the cell potential, it counteracts the driving force of the spontaneous redox reaction.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conditions
When the applied opposing external voltage is less than the cell potential (\(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\)), the spontaneous reaction continues, electrons flow from zinc to copper, and current flows from copper to zinc. When the external potential equals the cell potential (\(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)), the net driving potential is zero.

Step 3: Conclusion
At \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), no net electron transfer takes place across the external circuit, the current drops to zero, and the overall chemical reaction stops completely.

Final Conceptual Answer: No current flows through the circuit and the cell reaction stops altogether.

answer.text: No current flows and no chemical reaction takes place
Electrons flow from copper to zinc and zinc is deposited at the anode
Current flows from copper to zinc at an increased rate
Zinc continues to dissolve and copper continues to deposit normally

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Behavior of Daniell cell when external potential exceeds cell potential

questiontext.text: When an external opposing voltage \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\) is applied to a standard Daniell cell consisting of zinc and copper electrodes dipped in \(1\text{ M}\) solutions of their respective salts, the cell behaves as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A galvanic cell generates electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction. When an external opposing voltage exceeds the standard electromotive force of the galvanic cell (\(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\)), electrical energy from the external source forces the non-spontaneous reverse reaction to occur.

Step 2: Analysis of Polarity and Direction of Flow
Under the influence of the external source with \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\), electrons are pushed from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode. Consequently, conventional electric current flows from zinc to copper.

Step 3: Nature of Electrode Processes
At the zinc electrode, reduction takes place (\(\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Zn}\)), depositing zinc. At the copper electrode, oxidation takes place (\(\text{Cu} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^-\)), dissolving copper. The device now operates as an electrolytic cell.

Final Conceptual Answer: An electrolytic cell where electrons flow from copper to zinc, with zinc depositing at the zinc electrode and copper dissolving at the copper electrode.

answer.text: A galvanic cell where electrons flow from zinc to copper and zinc continues to dissolve
An electrolytic cell where electrons flow from copper to zinc, zinc deposits at the zinc electrode, and copper dissolves
An electrolytic cell where electrons flow from zinc to copper and copper dissolves
A galvanic cell operating at zero net potential with no chemical transformation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Current flow and electrode reactions in Daniell cell under low opposing voltage

questiontext.text: In a Daniell cell connected to an opposing external circuit with \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\), which of the following statements correctly describes the flow of current and the electrode processes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a galvanic cell, the spontaneous redox reaction is \(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\). Oxidation occurs at the zinc rod (anode) and reduction occurs at the copper rod (cathode).

Step 2: Direction of Current and Electron Flow
When the opposing external potential is less than \(1.1\text{ V}\) (\(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\)), the spontaneous cell reaction dominates. Electrons flow through the external circuit from the zinc rod to the copper rod, meaning conventional electric current flows from the copper rod to the zinc rod.

Step 3: Mass Changes at Electrodes
Zinc atoms lose electrons and dissolve into solution as \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) ions at the anode, while \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ions gain electrons and deposit as metallic copper at the cathode.

Final Conceptual Answer: Conventional current flows from copper to zinc, zinc dissolves at the anode, and copper deposits at the cathode.

answer.text: Current flows from zinc to copper, zinc deposits at the cathode, and copper dissolves at the anode
Electrons flow from copper to zinc, zinc dissolves at the anode, and copper deposits at the cathode
Current flows from copper to zinc, zinc dissolves at the anode, and copper deposits at the cathode
Current flows from copper to zinc, copper dissolves at the cathode, and zinc deposits at the anode

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Electrode polarity and IUPAC convention in galvanic cells

questiontext.text: According to IUPAC conventions for galvanic cells, which of the following statements correctly identifies the nature of the anode and cathode and their electrostatic potentials with respect to the solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Anode and Cathode
In any electrochemical cell, the electrode at which oxidation occurs is defined as the anode, and the electrode at which reduction occurs is defined as the cathode.

Step 2: Sign Conventions in Galvanic Cells
In a galvanic cell, metal atoms leave electrons on the anode as they oxidize into solution, giving the anode a negative potential relative to the solution. At the cathode, metal ions take up electrons from the electrode to get reduced, giving the cathode a positive potential relative to the solution.

Step 3: Conclusion
The anode is the site of oxidation and has a negative potential, while the cathode is the site of reduction and has a positive potential.

Final Conceptual Answer: The anode is the electrode where oxidation takes place and has a negative potential with respect to the solution, whereas the cathode is where reduction takes place and has a positive potential.

answer.text: Reduction occurs at the anode which has a negative potential, and oxidation occurs at the cathode which has a positive potential
Oxidation occurs at the cathode which has a negative potential, and reduction occurs at the anode which has a positive potential
Oxidation occurs at the anode which has a positive potential, and reduction occurs at the cathode which has a negative potential
Oxidation occurs at the anode which has a negative potential, and reduction occurs at the cathode which has a positive potential

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - IUPAC representation of copper silver galvanic cell

questiontext.text:
For the spontaneous cell reaction:

\[\text{Cu(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}\]

Which of the following represents the correct IUPAC cell formulation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Half-Reactions
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\text{Cu(s)} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\) (Anode process).
Reduction half-reaction: \(\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Ag(s)}\) (Cathode process).

Step 2: Apply IUPAC Cell Notation Rules
By IUPAC convention, the anode (oxidation half-cell) is written on the left and the cathode (reduction half-cell) is written on the right.
A single vertical line represents a phase boundary between the solid electrode and the electrolyte.
A double vertical line represents the salt bridge connecting the two electrolyte solutions.

Step 3: Construct Cell Representation
The oxidation half-cell is written as \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})\).
The reduction half-cell is written as \(\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\).
Joining them across the salt bridge gives: \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Calculation of standard electromotive force of copper silver cell

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials:

\[E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\]

What is the standard electromotive force (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potential of cathode (right electrode, silver): \(E^\circ_{\text{right}} = E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\).
Standard reduction potential of anode (left electrode, copper): \(E^\circ_{\text{left}} = E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard electrode potentials are reduction potentials according to IUPAC convention. The standard cell potential is the standard reduction potential of the cathode minus the standard reduction potential of the anode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{right}} - E^\circ_{\text{left}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.80\text{ V} - 0.34\text{ V} = +0.46\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since the cell reaction is spontaneous, \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) must be positive, which is confirmed as \(+0.46\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(+0.46\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Standard conditions and potential of the standard hydrogen electrode

questiontext.text: Which of the following conditions and arbitrary potential values correctly define the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard hydrogen electrode is the universal reference electrode used to measure standard electrode potentials of other redox couples.

Step 2: Operating Conditions
The standard hydrogen electrode consists of a platinum electrode coated with platinum black dipping in an acidic solution with a hydrogen ion concentration of \(1\text{ M}\) (\(1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\)), with pure hydrogen gas bubbled over it at a pressure of \(1\text{ bar}\).

Step 3: Conventional Potential
By international agreement and IUPAC convention, the potential of the standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a value of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at all temperatures.

Final Conceptual Answer: Hydrogen gas at \(1\text{ bar}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 1\text{ M}\), with an assigned potential of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at all temperatures.

answer.text: Hydrogen gas at \(1\text{ atm}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 0.1\text{ M}\), with an assigned potential of \(1.00\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\)
Hydrogen gas at \(1\text{ bar}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 1\text{ M}\), with a potential that varies linearly with temperature
Hydrogen gas at \(1\text{ bar}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 1\text{ M}\), with an assigned potential of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at all temperatures
Hydrogen gas at \(10\text{ bar}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 1\text{ M}\), with an assigned potential of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at \(0^\circ\text{C}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Role of inert platinum and gold electrodes in redox systems

questiontext.text: In electrochemical cells, inert electrodes such as platinum or gold are frequently employed (for example in \(\text{Pt(s)} \mid \text{H}_2(\text{g}) \mid \text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})\) or \(\text{Pt(s)} \mid \text{Br}_2(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\)). What is the primary function of these inert electrodes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An inert electrode is chemically unreactive under the operating conditions of the half-cell reaction.

Step 2: Function in Half-Cells
Metals like platinum and gold do not take part chemically in the oxidation or reduction reactions (they neither dissolve as ions nor do their cations deposit).

Step 3: Physical Role
They provide a solid conducting surface for the adsorption of reactants, catalyze electron transfer between chemical species, and facilitate the conduction of electrons to and from the external circuit.

Final Conceptual Answer: They provide a surface for oxidation or reduction reactions and conduct electrons without participating chemically in the reaction.

answer.text: They react with the electrolyte solution to generate additional electromotive force
They dissolve preferentially to maintain electrical neutrality in the half-cell
They prevent gas bubbles from forming and prevent electron transfer into the wire
They provide a surface for oxidation-reduction reactions and electron conduction without participating chemically

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Thermodynamic feasibility of ferric ion redox reactions with halides

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-} = +0.54\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-} = +1.09\text{ V}\]

Which of the following reactions is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ_{\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-} = +0.54\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-} = +1.09\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Criterion for Feasibility
A redox reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions if the overall standard cell potential is positive (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0\)), where \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{reduction}} - E^\circ_{\text{oxidation}}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{I}^-\)
For the reaction \(2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{I}_2\):
Reduction: \(\text{Fe}^{3+} + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}\), \(E^\circ = +0.77\text{ V}\).
Oxidation: \(2\text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), \(E^\circ = +0.54\text{ V}\).
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.77\text{ V} - 0.54\text{ V} = +0.23\text{ V} > 0\). This reaction is spontaneous and feasible.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Br}^-\)
For the reaction \(2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{Br}_2\):
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.77\text{ V} - 1.09\text{ V} = -0.32\text{ V} < 0\). This reaction is non-feasible.

Final Conceptual Answer: The reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) and \(\text{I}^-(\text{aq})\) is feasible, whereas the reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) and \(\text{Br}^-(\text{aq})\) is not feasible.

answer.text: Oxidation of \(\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is feasible, but oxidation of \(\text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is not feasible
Both the oxidation of \(\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq})\) and \(\text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) are feasible
Oxidation of \(\text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is feasible, but oxidation of \(\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is not feasible
Neither the oxidation of \(\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq})\) nor \(\text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is feasible

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Oxidizing and reducing power trends in electrochemical series

questiontext.text: According to the electrochemical series given in the NCERT textbook, lithium has the most negative standard reduction potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}} = -3.05\text{ V}\)) and fluorine has the most positive (\(E^\circ_{\text{F}_2/\text{F}^-} = +2.87\text{ V}\)). This implies that in aqueous solution:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard electrode potentials are listed as reduction potentials. A higher positive \(E^\circ\) indicates a greater tendency of the oxidized form to gain electrons (act as an oxidizing agent).

Step 2: Analysis of the Extreme Values
Fluorine has the highest positive potential (\(+2.87\text{ V}\)), indicating that \(\text{F}_2\) gas has the strongest tendency to be reduced to \(\text{F}^-\), making \(\text{F}_2\) the strongest oxidizing agent.

Step 3: Reducing Power of Lithium
Lithium has the most negative potential (\(-3.05\text{ V}\)), which means \(\text{Li}^+\) is the weakest oxidizing agent, and conversely, metallic lithium has the greatest tendency to lose electrons, making lithium metal the most powerful reducing agent in aqueous solution.

Final Conceptual Answer: Lithium metal is the strongest reducing agent and fluorine gas is the strongest oxidizing agent.

answer.text: Lithium ion is the strongest reducing agent and fluoride ion is the strongest oxidising agent
Lithium metal is the strongest reducing agent and fluorine gas is the strongest oxidising agent
Fluorine gas is the strongest reducing agent and lithium metal is the strongest oxidising agent
Lithium metal is the strongest oxidising agent and fluorine gas is the strongest reducing agent

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Displacement order of metals from salt solutions based on potentials

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[E^\circ_{\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}} = -2.36\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} = -0.44\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\]

Which of the following represents the correct order in which each metal can displace the succeeding metals from their aqueous salt solutions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Principle
A metal with a more negative standard reduction potential has a greater reducing power and can displace a metal with a less negative (or positive) reduction potential from its aqueous salt solution.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potentials
\(\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}\) (\(-2.36\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}\) (\(-1.66\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}\) (\(-0.76\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}\) (\(-0.44\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\) (\(+0.34\text{ V}\)).

Step 3: Establishing Displacement Order
Magnesium has the strongest reducing tendency and displaces aluminium, zinc, iron, and copper. Aluminium displaces zinc, iron, and copper. Zinc displaces iron and copper. Iron displaces copper. Thus, the order of displacing power is \(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Electrochemical basis of copper dissolution in nitric acid versus hydrochloric acid

questiontext.text: Metallic copper does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid to liberate hydrogen gas, but it readily dissolves in nitric acid. What is the fundamental electrochemical reason for this behavior?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Acid Dissolution
For a metal to dissolve in an acid by liberating hydrogen gas, the metal must be oxidized by \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions: \(\text{M} + n\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{M}^{n+} + \frac{n}{2}\text{H}_2\). This requires the standard reduction potential of the metal couple to be lower (more negative) than that of the \(\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2\) couple (\(0.00\text{ V}\)).

Step 2: Interaction with Hydrochloric Acid
The standard potential of copper is \(E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), which is positive relative to the standard hydrogen electrode. Therefore, \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions cannot oxidize metallic copper under standard conditions, so copper does not dissolve in \(\text{HCl}\).

Step 3: Interaction with Nitric Acid
Nitric acid contains nitrate ions (\(\text{NO}_3^-\)), which have a much higher standard reduction potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{NO}_3^-/\text{NO}} = +0.97\text{ V}\)) than \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\) (\(+0.34\text{ V}\)). Copper is oxidized by the nitrate ion rather than by the hydrogen ion.

Final Conceptual Answer: Copper has a positive reduction potential and cannot be oxidized by \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions, but is oxidized by nitrate ions in nitric acid.

answer.text: Nitric acid is a much weaker acid than \(\text{HCl}\), which prevents passivation of copper
Copper forms an insoluble chloride film with \(\text{HCl}\) that halts the dissolution reaction
Chloride ions reduce copper ions back to metallic copper more rapidly than hydrogen gas can evolve
Copper has a positive \(E^\circ\) relative to hydrogen so \(\text{H}^{+}\) cannot oxidise it, but nitrate ions in \(\text{HNO}_3\) can oxidise it

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Calculation of cell potential using Nernst equation for magnesium silver cell

questiontext.text:
A galvanic cell operates based on the reaction:

\[\text{Mg(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(0.0001\text{ M}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(0.130\text{ M}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}\]

Given that \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\), what is the electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\).
Electrode reaction: \(\text{Mg(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}\).
Number of electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Concentrations: \([\text{Mg}^{2+}] = 0.130\text{ M}\), \([\text{Ag}^{+}] = 0.0001\text{ M} = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Apply the Nernst equation at \(T = 298\text{ K}\) where solid magnesium and silver have activities equal to unity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\text{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the reaction quotient term:
\[Q = \frac{[\text{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2} = \frac{0.130}{(10^{-4})^2} = \frac{0.130}{10^{-8}} = 1.30 \times 10^7\]
Evaluate the logarithm:
\[\log(1.30 \times 10^7) = \log(1.30) + 7 \approx 0.1139 + 7 = 7.114\]
Calculate the subtraction term:
\[\frac{0.059}{2} \times 7.114 \approx 0.0295 \times 7.114 \approx 0.21\text{ V}\]
Substitute into the Nernst equation:
\[E_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V} - 0.21\text{ V} = 2.96\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The potential decreases from \(3.17\text{ V}\) to \(2.96\text{ V}\) because the reaction quotient \(Q > 1\), as expected from Le Chatelier's principle and Nernst equation.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(2.96\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Effect of ion concentrations on Daniell cell potential

questiontext.text:
For the Daniell cell operating at \(298\text{ K}\) according to the reaction:

\[\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\]

How does the cell electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) vary when the concentration of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ions is increased while the concentration of \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) ions is decreased?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principle and Formula
The Nernst equation for the Daniell cell at \(298\text{ K}\) is given by: \[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\]

Step 2: Analysis of the Concentration Ratio
The logarithmic term depends directly on the ratio of product ion concentration to reactant ion concentration: \(Q = \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\).
When \([\text{Cu}^{2+}]\) increases and \([\text{Zn}^{2+}]\) decreases, the reaction quotient \(Q\) decreases significantly.

Step 3: Effect on Cell Potential
As \(Q\) decreases, \(\log Q\) becomes smaller (or more negative), which reduces the value being subtracted from \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) (or adds to it). Consequently, the value of \(E_{\text{cell}}\) increases.

Final Conceptual Answer: The cell potential increases when the copper ion concentration increases and the zinc ion concentration decreases.

answer.text: The cell potential remains strictly constant at \(1.10\text{ V}\)
The cell potential drops to zero immediately

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Electrode potential calculation of hydrogen electrode at specified pH

questiontext.text: What is the electrode potential of a hydrogen electrode at \(298\text{ K}\) dipping in an aqueous solution of \(\text{pH} = 10\) under a hydrogen gas pressure of \(1\text{ bar}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\text{pH} = 10\).
Hydrogen gas pressure: \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 1\text{ bar}\).
Temperature: \(T = 298\text{ K}\).
Electrode reaction (reduction): \(\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g})\).
Standard reduction potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = 0.00\text{ V}\).
Number of electrons: \(n = 1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Activity of pure gas at \(1\text{ bar}\) is unity. From the definition of pH, \([\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-10}\text{ M}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
By Nernst equation for the hydrogen electrode reduction: \[E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} - \frac{0.059}{1} \log \frac{1}{[\text{H}^{+}]}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(E^\circ = 0\text{ V}\) and \([\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-10}\text{ M}\): \[E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = 0 - 0.059 \log \frac{1}{10^{-10}} = -0.059 \log(10^{10})\] \[E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = -0.059 \times 10 = -0.59\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \([\text{H}^{+}]\) is much lower than standard \(1\text{ M}\), reduction of \(\text{H}^{+}\) is less favorable than under standard conditions, resulting in a negative electrode potential of \(-0.59\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(-0.59\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - General Nernst equation formulation for multi electron cell reactions

questiontext.text:
For a general electrochemical reaction occurring in a galvanic cell:

\[a\text{A} + b\text{B} \xrightarrow{n\mathrm{e}^-} c\text{C} + d\text{D}\]

Which of the following represents the correct general Nernst equation for the cell potential at temperature \(T\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Nernst equation relates the cell potential under non-standard conditions to the standard cell potential, the temperature, the number of moles of electrons transferred, and the reaction quotient \(Q\).

Step 2: Formulation of Reaction Quotient
For the general reaction \(a\text{A} + b\text{B} \rightarrow c\text{C} + d\text{D}\), the reaction quotient in terms of molar concentrations is: \[Q = \frac{[\text{C}]^c [\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a [\text{B}]^b}\]

Step 3: General Expression
Substituting the reaction quotient into the thermodynamic relation gives: \[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{nF} \ln \frac{[\text{C}]^c [\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a [\text{B}]^b}\]

Final Conceptual Answer: \(E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{RT}{nF} \ln \frac{[\text{C}]^c [\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a [\text{B}]^b}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q17 - Calculation of electromotive force for nickel silver galvanic cell

questiontext.text:
Calculate the electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell at \(298\text{ K}\) in which the following reaction takes place:

\[\text{Ni(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(0.002\text{ M}) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(0.160\text{ M}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}\]

Given: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.05\text{ V}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(\text{Ni(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + 2\text{Ag(s)}\).
Number of electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Standard potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.05\text{ V}\).
Concentrations: \([\text{Ni}^{2+}] = 0.160\text{ M}\), \([\text{Ag}^{+}] = 0.002\text{ M} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluate the concentration ratio term: \[[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2 = (2 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 4 \times 10^{-6}\] \[\frac{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2} = \frac{0.160}{4 \times 10^{-6}} = 4 \times 10^4\] Take the base-10 logarithm: \[\log(4 \times 10^4) = \log 4 + 4 \approx 0.6021 + 4 = 4.6021\] Calculate the logarithmic deduction: \[\frac{0.059}{2} \times 4.6021 \approx 0.0295 \times 4.6021 \approx 0.1358\text{ V} \approx 0.14\text{ V}\] Calculate cell potential: \[E_{\text{cell}} = 1.05\text{ V} - 0.14\text{ V} = 0.91\text{ V}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The cell potential decreases below the standard potential due to product accumulation, giving \(0.91\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0.91\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Attainment of electrochemical equilibrium in a working galvanic cell

questiontext.text: When the external circuit of a working Daniell cell is kept closed for a prolonged time, what happens to the cell potential, the concentrations of \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\), and the electrical state of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As the galvanic cell discharges, the forward reaction consumes \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) and generates \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\). According to the Nernst equation, this progressive change in concentrations causes the reaction quotient to increase, which lowers the cell potential.

Step 2: Achievement of Dynamic Equilibrium
Eventually, a state of dynamic chemical equilibrium is reached where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.

Step 3: Equilibrium Values
At equilibrium, there is no further change in the concentrations of \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\), the net driving force drops to zero, the cell potential becomes \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\text{ V}\), and current ceases to flow.

Final Conceptual Answer: The cell potential becomes zero, concentrations of ions reach equilibrium values, and no current flows.

answer.text: The cell potential reaches its maximum value of \(1.10\text{ V}\) and remains constant
The cell potential drops to zero, the ion concentrations stop changing, and the current ceases
The copper ion concentration reaches zero while the cell potential remains positive
The cell polarity reverses spontaneously with current flowing in the opposite direction

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q19 - Equilibrium constant evaluation from standard cell potential of Daniell cell

questiontext.text:
For the Daniell cell reaction at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\]

Given that the standard cell potential is \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\), what is the value of the equilibrium constant (\(K_c\)) of the reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\).
Number of electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Constant: \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\) at \(T = 298\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
At equilibrium, \(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\), which gives: \[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{0.059}{n} \log K_c\] \[\log K_c = \frac{n E^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.059}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\[\log K_c = \frac{2 \times 1.1\text{ V}}{0.059\text{ V}} = \frac{2.2}{0.059} \approx 37.288\] Taking antilogarithm: \[K_c = 10^{37.288} = 10^{0.288} \times 10^{37} \approx 1.94 \times 10^{37} \approx 2 \times 10^{37}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
A large positive \(E^\circ\) corresponds to an enormous equilibrium constant, indicating the reaction goes virtually to completion.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(2 \times 10^{37}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q20 - Standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant for ferric iodide redox reaction

questiontext.text:
For the redox reaction at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[2\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{I}_2(\text{s})\]

The standard cell potential is \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}\). Taking \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\), what are the standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) and the equilibrium constant (\(K_c\)) of the reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(2\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{I}_2(\text{s})\).
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}\).
Electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\] \[\log K_c = \frac{n E^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{0.059\text{ V}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(\Delta_r G^\circ\): \[\Delta_r G^\circ = -2 \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 0.236\text{ V} = -45541.86\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx -45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\] Calculate \(\log K_c\): \[\log K_c = \frac{2 \times 0.236}{0.059} = \frac{0.472}{0.059} = 8.0\] Taking antilogarithm: \[K_c = 10^8 \text{ (or } 9.62 \times 10^7 \text{ using exact } 0.05916\text{ V)}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Standard Gibbs energy is \(-45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and equilibrium constant is \(9.62 \times 10^7\) (order of \(10^8\)).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\Delta_r G^\circ = -45.54\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(K_c = 9.62 \times 10^7\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q21 - Fundamental relation between standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

questiontext.text: Which of the following equations correctly expresses the thermodynamic relationship between the standard Gibbs energy of a cell reaction (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) and its equilibrium constant (\(K\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum electrical work done reversibly by a galvanic cell is equal to the decrease in Gibbs free energy: \(\Delta_r G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}\). Under standard conditions, \(\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\).

Step 2: Linking to Equilibrium Constant
At equilibrium, the driving potential of the cell becomes zero (\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\)). The Nernst equation yields: \[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \frac{RT}{nF} \ln K\]

Step 3: Substitution
Multiplying both sides by \(-nF\): \[-nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -RT \ln K\] \[\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT \ln K\]

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT \ln K\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q22 - Relation between reversible electrical work and Gibbs energy decrease

questiontext.text: If a galvanic cell has an electromotive force \(E_{\text{cell}}\) and delivers an amount of charge \(nF\) reversibly, what is the relationship between the decrease in its Gibbs free energy (\(-\Delta_r G\)) and the reversible electrical work done (\(W_{\text{elec}}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrical work done is equal to electrical potential multiplied by total charge passed: \[W_{\text{elec}} = \text{Charge} \times \text{Potential} = nF E_{\text{cell}}\]

Step 2: Thermodynamic Definition
According to thermodynamics, the reversible electrical work obtained from a system operating at constant temperature and pressure equals the decrease in its Gibbs free energy: \[W_{\text{rev}} = -\Delta_r G\]

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the decrease in Gibbs energy is directly equal to the maximum electrical work done by the cell: \(\Delta_r G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: Reversible electrical work is equal to the decrease in Gibbs free energy, giving \(W_{\text{elec}} = -\Delta_r G = nFE_{\text{cell}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q23 - Standard Gibbs energy change calculation for standard Daniell cell

questiontext.text: The standard cell potential for the Daniell cell reaction \(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\) is \(1.10\text{ V}\). Taking \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\), what is the standard Gibbs energy (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) for this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V}\).
Number of electrons: \(n = 2\).
Faraday constant: \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Delta_r G^\circ = -2 \times 1.10\text{ V} \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\] \[\Delta_r G^\circ = -212271.4\text{ J mol}^{-1} \approx -212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since the cell reaction is spontaneous, \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) is negative, corresponding to \(-212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(-212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q24 - Intensive and extensive nature of cell potential and Gibbs energy

questiontext.text:
Consider the two balanced chemical equations for the Daniell cell:

Reaction 1: \(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\)

Reaction 2: \(2\text{Zn(s)} + 2\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + 2\text{Cu(s)}\)

How do the standard cell potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) and standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) compare between Reaction 1 and Reaction 2?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
Electrode potential and cell potential (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) are intensive properties, meaning their values do not depend on the size of the system or the stoichiometric coefficients chosen to write the reaction equation.
Gibbs free energy change (\(\Delta_r G\)) is an extensive thermodynamic property, meaning its value depends directly on the amount of substance reacting (proportional to stoichiometric coefficients and the number of moles of electrons transferred, \(n\)).

Step 2: Comparison for the Two Reactions
For Reaction 1: \(n = 2\), so \(E^\circ_1 = 1.1\text{ V}\) and \(\Delta_r G^\circ_1 = -2FE^\circ\).
For Reaction 2: \(n = 4\), so \(E^\circ_2 = 1.1\text{ V}\) and \(\Delta_r G^\circ_2 = -4FE^\circ = 2\Delta_r G^\circ_1\).

Step 3: Conclusion
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) remains identical for both equations, while \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) for Reaction 2 is twice that of Reaction 1.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) is identical for both reactions because it is an intensive property, but \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) doubles for Reaction 2 because it is an extensive property.

answer.text: Both \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) and \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) double for Reaction 2 compared to Reaction 1
\(\Delta_r G^\circ\) is the same for both reactions, but \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) doubles for Reaction 2
Both \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) and \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) remain completely unchanged because they are both intensive properties
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) is the same for both reactions, but \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) for Reaction 2 is twice that of Reaction 1

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q25 - Temperature dependence of metallic versus electrolytic electrical conductance

questiontext.text: How does electrical conductance change with an increase in temperature for metallic (electronic) conductors and electrolytic (ionic) solutions, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Metallic Conductance
In metallic conductors, current is carried by mobile free electrons moving through a lattice of positive metal ions (kernels). As temperature rises, thermal vibrations of the metal kernels increase, which impedes the flow of electrons through increased scattering. Hence, metallic conductance decreases with increasing temperature.

Step 2: Mechanism of Electrolytic Conductance
In electrolytic solutions, current is carried by ions moving through a solvent. As temperature increases: (i) the viscosity of the solvent decreases, reducing drag on moving ions; (ii) the kinetic energy and mobility of ions increase; (iii) the degree of dissociation of weak electrolytes increases. Hence, electrolytic conductance increases with increasing temperature.

Step 3: Conclusion
Metallic conductance decreases with increasing temperature, whereas electrolytic conductance increases with increasing temperature.

Final Conceptual Answer: Metallic conductance decreases while electrolytic conductance increases with increase in temperature.

answer.text: Metallic conductance decreases while electrolytic conductance increases with increase in temperature
Metallic conductance increases while electrolytic conductance decreases with increase in temperature
Both metallic and electrolytic conductance increase with increase in temperature
Both metallic and electrolytic conductance decrease with increase in temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q26 - SI unit and conversion relation for electrolytic conductivity

questiontext.text: What is the SI unit of electrolytic conductivity (\(\kappa\)), and how is it related to its commonly used submultiple unit \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Conductivity
Conductivity (\(\kappa\)) is the reciprocal of electrical resistivity (\(\rho\)): \[\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho}\] Since resistivity has the SI unit \(\Omega\text{ m}\), conductivity has the SI unit \(\Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: SI Unit of Conductance
In the SI system, \(\Omega^{-1}\) is named siemens (\(\text{S}\)). Thus, the SI unit of conductivity is \(\text{S m}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Conversion to Submultiple Unit
\[1\text{ S cm}^{-1} = \frac{1\text{ S}}{10^{-2}\text{ m}} = 100\text{ S m}^{-1}\] Equivalently, \(1\text{ S m}^{-1} = 0.01\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: The SI unit is \(\text{S m}^{-1}\), and \(1\text{ S cm}^{-1} = 100\text{ S m}^{-1}\).

answer.text: \(\text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), where \(1\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q27 - Characteristics and applications of organic conducting polymers

questiontext.text: In 1977, MacDiarmid, Heeger, and Shirakawa discovered that exposure of polyacetylene to iodine vapors imparts metallic lustre and electrical conductivity. Which of the following statements regarding conducting polymers is correct based on the textbook discussion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain organic polymers possessing conjugated pi-electron backbones can be doped (e.g., polyacetylene exposed to iodine vapors) to acquire high electrical conductivity and metallic lustre.

Step 2: Examples and Composition
Examples of organic conducting polymers include polyacetylene, polyaniline, polypyrrole, and polythiophene. These materials are composed wholly of light elements like carbon, hydrogen, and occasionally nitrogen, oxygen, or sulfur.

Step 3: Properties and Practical Advantages
Because they are polymers, they are significantly lighter than conventional metals and possess mechanical flexibility, allowing them to be utilized in lightweight batteries and flexible electronic devices such as plastic transistors.

Final Conceptual Answer: Organic conducting polymers like polyaniline and polypyrrole are much lighter than metals, mechanically flexible, and can be used in lightweight batteries and flexible electronics.

answer.text: They are heavy inorganic alloys with zero electrical resistance at room temperature
They conduct electricity via ionic migration and permanently degrade upon current passage
They are composed of light elements, offer mechanical flexibility, and are suitable for lightweight batteries
They act as electrical insulators that block electron flow in solid-state devices

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q28 - Factors influencing ionic conductance in electrolytic solutions

questiontext.text: The electrolytic (ionic) conductance of a solution depends on several specific factors. Which of the following factors does NOT increase the conductivity of an electrolytic solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrolytic conductance arises from the movement of ions under an applied electric field.

Step 2: Analysis of Factors
(i) Increase in temperature increases ion mobility and decreases solvent viscosity, thereby increasing conductance.
(ii) Smaller effective size of hydrated ions facilitates faster migration, increasing conductance.
(iii) Higher dielectric constant of solvent favors ion dissociation, increasing conductance.
(iv) Increase in solvent viscosity increases viscous drag on ions, which retards their movement and decreases conductance.

Step 3: Conclusion
Higher solvent viscosity decreases ion mobility and therefore decreases electrolytic conductivity.

Final Conceptual Answer: High viscosity of the solvent decreases electrolytic conductivity.

answer.text: Increase in temperature of the electrolytic solution
Decrease in the size of the solvated ions
Higher degree of dissociation of the added electrolyte

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q29 - Determination and significance of conductivity cell constant

questiontext.text: In a conductivity cell with electrodes of cross-sectional area \(A\) separated by a distance \(l\), the cell constant \(G^*\) is defined as \(\frac{l}{A}\). Why is the cell constant usually determined by measuring the resistance with standard \(\text{KCl}\) solutions rather than by direct measurement of \(l\) and \(A\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cell constant is defined geometrically as \(G^* = \frac{l}{A}\), having the dimension of \(\text{length}^{-1}\) (measured in \(\text{m}^{-1}\) or \(\text{cm}^{-1}\)).

Step 2: Practical Limitations of Direct Measurement
In practical conductivity cells, measuring the exact distance \(l\) between platinized electrodes and their effective surface area \(A\) is not only inconvenient but also unreliable due to electrode roughness, coating porosity, and irregular cell geometry.

Step 3: Standard Calibration Method
The cell constant is reliably determined by measuring the resistance \(R\) of the cell when filled with a standard solution of potassium chloride (\(\text{KCl}\)) whose conductivity \(\kappa\) has been precisely determined at that temperature: \[G^* = R \times \kappa\]

Final Conceptual Answer: Direct measurement of electrode distance and area is inconvenient and unreliable, whereas calibration with standard \(\text{KCl}\) of known conductivity provides high accuracy.

answer.text: Direct geometric measurement of distance and area is inconvenient and unreliable
The cell constant changes continuously with every new electrolyte measured
Standard potassium chloride reacts chemically with platinum electrodes to fix their area
Cell constant has no physical dimensions and cannot be measured with physical instruments

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q30 - Rationale for using alternating current in electrolytic resistance measurement

questiontext.text: When measuring the electrical resistance of an electrolytic solution using a Wheatstone bridge, an alternating current (AC) source in the audio frequency range is used instead of a direct current (DC) source. What is the reason for this choice?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Wheatstone bridge is designed to measure electrical resistance. However, an electrolytic solution conducts via the movement of ions rather than electrons.

Step 2: Effect of Direct Current
Passing direct current (DC) through an electrolytic solution causes continuous electrolysis and polarization at the electrodes, changing the composition and concentration of the solution and setting up an opposing back-emf.

Step 3: Effect of Alternating Current
Using an alternating current (AC) power source (typically 550 to 5000 cycles per second) continuously alternates the direction of current, preventing net chemical transformation, polarization, and changes in the solution composition.

Final Conceptual Answer: Passing direct current causes electrolysis and changes the chemical composition of the solution.

answer.text: Alternating current converts the electrolytic solution into a metallic conductor
Passing direct current causes electrolysis and alters the composition of the solution
Direct current cannot be detected by any Wheatstone bridge detector or headphone
Alternating current eliminates resistance entirely, allowing direct reading of conductance

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q31 - Relationship and conversion between units of molar conductivity

questiontext.text: Molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) is defined as the ratio of conductivity (\(\kappa\)) to concentration (\(c\)). Which of the following equations correctly expresses the relationship between the numerical values of \(\Lambda_m\) in \(\text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Molar Conductivity
Molar conductivity is defined by: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c}\]

Step 2: Dimensional Unit Conversion
In SI units, \(\Lambda_m\) is expressed in \(\text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\). In common laboratory units, it is expressed in \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
Since \(1\text{ m} = 100\text{ cm}\), we have: \[1\text{ m}^2 = (100\text{ cm})^2 = 10^4\text{ cm}^2\] Therefore: \[1\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 3: Reciprocal Relation
Equivalently: \[1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Final Conceptual Answer: \(1\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

answer.text: \(1\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^2\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(1\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 10^4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q32 - Conductivity and molar conductivity computation for potassium chloride solution

questiontext.text: The resistance of a conductivity cell filled with \(0.1\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution is \(100\ \Omega\). When the same cell is filled with \(0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution, the measured resistance is \(520\ \Omega\). Given that the conductivity of \(0.1\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution is \(1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\), what are the conductivity and molar conductivity of the \(0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ KCl}\) solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Resistance with \(0.1\text{ M KCl}\): \(R_1 = 100\ \Omega\).
Conductivity of \(0.1\text{ M KCl}\): \(\kappa_1 = 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1}\).
Resistance with \(0.02\text{ M KCl}\): \(R_2 = 520\ \Omega\).
Concentration: \(c_2 = 0.02\text{ mol L}^{-1} = 20\text{ mol m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[G^* = R_1 \kappa_1\] \[\kappa_2 = \frac{G^*}{R_2}\] \[\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa_2}{c_2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate cell constant: \[G^* = 1.29\text{ S m}^{-1} \times 100\ \Omega = 129\text{ m}^{-1} = 1.29\text{ cm}^{-1}\] Calculate conductivity of \(0.02\text{ M KCl}\): \[\kappa_2 = \frac{129\text{ m}^{-1}}{520\ \Omega} \approx 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\] Calculate molar conductivity in SI units: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}}{20\text{ mol m}^{-3}} = 1.24 \times 10^{-2}\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\] Converting to \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\): \[\Lambda_m = 124 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^4 = 124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The conductivity is \(0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\) and molar conductivity is \(124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\kappa = 0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\) and \(\Lambda_m = 124\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

answer.text: \(\kappa = 2.48\text{ S m}^{-1}\) and \(\Lambda_m = 12.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q33 - Resistivity conductivity and molar conductivity calculation of sodium hydroxide column

questiontext.text: The electrical resistance of a cylindrical column of \(0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}\text{ NaOH}\) solution of diameter \(1\text{ cm}\) and length \(50\text{ cm}\) is \(5.55 \times 10^3\ \Omega\). What are its resistivity (\(\rho\)), conductivity (\(\kappa\)), and molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) in \(\text{cm}\)-based units?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration: \(c = 0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).
Diameter: \(d = 1\text{ cm} \implies \text{radius } r = 0.5\text{ cm}\).
Length: \(l = 50\text{ cm}\).
Resistance: \(R = 5.55 \times 10^3\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
Area: \(A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (0.5)^2 = 0.785\text{ cm}^2\).
Resistivity: \(\rho = \frac{R A}{l}\).
Conductivity: \(\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho}\).
Molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate resistivity: \[\rho = \frac{5.55 \times 10^3\ \Omega \times 0.785\text{ cm}^2}{50\text{ cm}} = 87.135\ \Omega\text{ cm}\] Calculate conductivity: \[\kappa = \frac{1}{87.135\ \Omega\text{ cm}} \approx 0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\] Calculate molar conductivity: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\text{ cm}^3\text{ L}^{-1}}{0.05\text{ mol L}^{-1}} = 229.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(\rho = 87.14\ \Omega\text{ cm}\), \(\kappa = 0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\), \(\Lambda_m = 229.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\rho = 87.14\ \Omega\text{ cm}\), \(\kappa = 0.01148\text{ S cm}^{-1}\), \(\Lambda_m = 229.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q34 - Fundamental reason for conductivity decrease upon electrolytic dilution

questiontext.text: Why does the conductivity (\(\kappa\)) of an electrolytic solution always decrease upon dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Conductivity
Conductivity (\(\kappa\)) is defined as the conductance of unit volume (\(1\text{ m}^3\) or \(1\text{ cm}^3\)) of an electrolytic solution placed between electrodes of unit cross-sectional area separated by unit distance.

Step 2: Effect of Dilution
When a solution is diluted by adding more solvent, the total volume increases while the number of moles of electrolyte remains fixed (or dissociates only partially more in weak electrolytes).

Step 3: Number of Current Carriers per Unit Volume
As a result of the volume increase, the number of current-carrying ions present per unit volume of solution decreases. Since conductivity depends directly on the concentration of charge carriers per unit volume, conductivity always decreases with dilution.

Final Conceptual Answer: The number of ions per unit volume that carry electric current decreases upon dilution.

answer.text: The speed of ionic migration drops to zero as solvent is added
The number of current-carrying ions per unit volume decreases upon dilution
The degree of dissociation of the electrolyte decreases drastically on dilution
The total volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte decreases

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q35 - Opposing effects governing molar conductivity increase during dilution

questiontext.text: While conductivity (\(\kappa\)) decreases on dilution, molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) increases with decrease in concentration. Which of the following statements correctly explains this phenomenon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molar conductivity is related to conductivity and volume by: \[\Lambda_m = \kappa V\] where \(V\) is the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte.

Step 2: Interplay Between Conductivity and Volume
On dilution, the conductivity \(\kappa\) decreases because the number of ions per unit volume decreases. However, the volume \(V\) containing one mole of electrolyte increases simultaneously.

Step 3: Dominance of Volume Expansion
Experimental observations establish that the increase in volume \(V\) on dilution more than compensates for the decrease in \(\kappa\). Additionally, for weak electrolytes, dilution increases the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)), further increasing the total number of ions produced per mole of electrolyte.

Final Conceptual Answer: The decrease in conductivity on dilution is more than compensated by the increase in the volume containing one mole of electrolyte.

answer.text: Conductivity increases while the volume containing one mole remains unchanged
The solvent molecules completely dissociate into ions, providing all electrical conductance
The decrease in conductivity is more than compensated by the increase in volume containing one mole of electrolyte
Electrode resistance drops to zero due to surface passivation by water molecules

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q36 - Physical determinants of Debye Huckel Onsager slope constant

questiontext.text:
For strong electrolytes, the variation of molar conductivity with concentration is described by the equation:

\[\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\]

What determines the value of the constant \(A\) for a given solvent and temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation models the concentration dependence of molar conductivity for strong electrolytes: \[\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\]

Step 2: Physical Basis of Constant \(A\)
The slope constant \(A\) arises from interionic attractions (electrophoretic and relaxation effects) that retard the movement of ions as concentration increases.

Step 3: Dependence on Electrolyte Type
For a specified solvent and temperature, the value of \(A\) depends strictly on the charges of the cation and anion produced upon dissociation (i.e., the valence type of the electrolyte). All electrolytes of a given stoichiometric charge type—such as 1-1 electrolytes (\(\text{NaCl}, \text{KCl}\)), 2-1 electrolytes (\(\text{CaCl}_2\)), or 2-2 electrolytes (\(\text{MgSO}_4\))—have the same value of \(A\).

Final Conceptual Answer: The type of electrolyte, specifically the charges on the cation and anion produced on dissociation.

answer.text: The atomic mass of the metallic element present in the salt
The shape and dimensions of the conductivity cell electrodes
The frequency of the alternating current source used in the bridge
The charges on the cation and anion produced upon dissociation of the electrolyte

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q37 - Graphical interpretation of intercept and slope in Onsager plots

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the variation of molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) with \(c^{1/2}\) for aqueous solutions of \(\text{KCl}\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\):

When the molar conductivities (\(\Lambda_m\)) of aqueous \(\text{KCl}\) solutions at \(298\text{ K}\) are plotted against \(c^{1/2}\), a straight line is obtained according to \(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\). From such a linear plot, the y-intercept at \(c^{1/2} = 0\) and the negative of the slope represent:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mathematical Model
The Debye-Hückel-Onsager relation for a strong electrolyte is: \[\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\] Comparing this to the standard linear equation \(y = mx + c\): \(y = \Lambda_m\), \(x = c^{1/2}\), slope \(m = -A\), and y-intercept \(= \Lambda_m^\circ\).

Step 2: Interpretation of the Intercept
At \(c^{1/2} = 0\) (which corresponds to concentration approaching zero, or infinite dilution), the y-intercept represents the limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) (for \(\text{KCl}\), \(\Lambda_m^\circ = 150.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Interpretation of the Slope
The slope of the line is negative (\(-A\)). Therefore, the negative of the slope gives the Onsager constant \(A\) (for \(\text{KCl}\), \(A = 87.46\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} / (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\)).

Final Conceptual Answer: The intercept represents the limiting molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) and the negative of the slope represents the constant \(A\).

answer.text: The limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) and the constant \(A\), respectively
The constant \(A\) and the limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^\circ\), respectively
The degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) and the dissociation constant \(K_a\), respectively
The cell constant \(G^*\) and the specific resistance \(\rho\), respectively

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q38 - Limiting molar conductivity calculation for calcium chloride and magnesium sulphate

questiontext.text:
Given the limiting molar conductivities of individual ions at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[\lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) = 119.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}, \quad \lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 76.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

\[\lambda^\circ(\text{Mg}^{2+}) = 106.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}, \quad \lambda^\circ(\text{SO}_4^{2-}) = 160.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

What are the limiting molar conductivities (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) of \(\text{CaCl}_2\) and \(\text{MgSO}_4\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual contributions of its constituent cations and anions: \[\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+ \lambda_+^\circ + \nu_- \lambda_-^\circ\]

Step 2: Calculation for Calcium Chloride
\(\text{CaCl}_2\) dissociates into one \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) and two \(\text{Cl}^-\) ions (\(\nu_+ = 1, \nu_- = 2\)): \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-)\] \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 119.0 + 152.6 = 271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 3: Calculation for Magnesium Sulphate
\(\text{MgSO}_4\) dissociates into one \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) and one \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) ion (\(\nu_+ = 1, \nu_- = 1\)): \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{MgSO}_4) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Mg}^{2+}) + \lambda^\circ(\text{SO}_4^{2-})\] \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{MgSO}_4) = 106.0 + 160.0 = 266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Final Conceptual Answer: \(271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) for \(\text{CaCl}_2\) and \(266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) for \(\text{MgSO}_4\).

answer.text: \(195.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and \(266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q39 - Impossibility of direct graphical extrapolation for weak electrolyte limiting conductivity

questiontext.text: Why can the limiting molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) of a weak electrolyte like acetic acid NOT be determined experimentally by extrapolating the plot of \(\Lambda_m\) versus \(c^{1/2}\) to zero concentration?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Weak Electrolyte Dissociation
Weak electrolytes have low degree of dissociation (\(\alpha \ll 1\)) at moderate concentrations. As dilution increases, Ostwald's dilution law dictates that \(\alpha\) increases, dramatically increasing the number of ions per mole of electrolyte.

Step 2: Graphical Behavior Near Zero Concentration
Near infinite dilution (very low concentrations), \(\Lambda_m\) increases very steeply (the curve approaches the y-axis almost vertically). Consequently, there is no linear portion to extrapolate to the y-axis at \(c = 0\).

Step 3: Practical Measurement Limitations
At extremely high dilution where dissociation is complete, the concentration of ions is so low that the conductivity of the solution becomes too small to be measured accurately.

Final Conceptual Answer: Molar conductivity increases very steeply at low concentrations so the curve cannot be linearly extrapolated, and conductivity becomes too low to measure accurately.

answer.text: Weak electrolytes completely decompose into neutral gas molecules at low concentration
The cell constant becomes zero at concentrations below one millimolar
Molar conductivity increases steeply at low concentrations, preventing linear extrapolation
Acetic acid undergoes irreversible oxidation at the platinum electrodes upon dilution

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q40 - Calculation of limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid using Kohlrausch law

questiontext.text: The limiting molar conductivities (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) at \(298\text{ K}\) for \(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{HCl}\), and \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\) (sodium acetate) are \(126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), \(425.9\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), and \(91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), respectively. What is the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl}) = 425.9\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) = 91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl}) = 126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Formula
By Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-)\] Expressing this in terms of strong electrolytes: \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) - \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = 425.9\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} + 91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} - 126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\] \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = 516.9 - 126.4 = 390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid is \(390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q41 - Degree of dissociation and acid dissociation constant determination from conductivity

questiontext.text: The conductivity of \(0.001028\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) acetic acid solution is \(4.95 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\). Given that \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) for acetic acid is \(390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), what are its degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) and dissociation constant (\(K_a\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration: \(c = 0.001028\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).
Conductivity: \(\kappa = 4.95 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).
Limiting molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_m^\circ = 390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\] \[\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}\] \[K_a = \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate molar conductivity: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{4.95 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\text{ cm}^3\text{ L}^{-1}}{0.001028\text{ mol L}^{-1}} = \frac{0.0495}{0.001028} \approx 48.15\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\] Calculate degree of dissociation: \[\alpha = \frac{48.15}{390.5} \approx 0.1233\] Calculate dissociation constant: \[K_a = \frac{0.001028 \times (0.1233)^2}{1 - 0.1233} = \frac{0.001028 \times 0.015203}{0.8767} \approx 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(\alpha = 0.1233\) and \(K_a = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\alpha = 0.1233\) and \(K_a = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q42 - Dissociation constant and degree of ionization of methanoic acid

questiontext.text: The molar conductivity of \(0.025\text{ mol L}^{-1}\) methanoic acid (\(\text{HCOOH}\)) is \(46.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\). Given that \(\lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) = 349.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\lambda^\circ(\text{HCOO}^-) = 54.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), what are its degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) and dissociation constant (\(K_a\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concentration: \(c = 0.025\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).
Molar conductivity: \(\Lambda_m = 46.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
Limiting ionic conductivities: \(\lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) = 349.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\), \(\lambda^\circ(\text{HCOO}^-) = 54.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCOOH}) = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{HCOO}^-)\] \[\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}\] \[K_a = \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate limiting molar conductivity: \[\Lambda_m^\circ = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\] Calculate degree of dissociation: \[\alpha = \frac{46.1}{404.2} \approx 0.11405 \approx 0.114\] Calculate dissociation constant: \[K_a = \frac{0.025 \times (0.114)^2}{1 - 0.114} = \frac{0.025 \times 0.012996}{0.886} = \frac{0.0003249}{0.886} \approx 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(\alpha = 0.114\) and \(K_a = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\alpha = 0.114\) and \(K_a = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q43 - Definition and magnitude of Faraday constant of electrical charge

questiontext.text: The quantity of electricity called Faraday (\(F\)) represents the magnitude of electrical charge carried by one mole of electrons. Taking the charge on a single electron as \(1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\) and Avogadro's constant as \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), what is the exact value of \(F\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
One mole of electrons consists of Avogadro's number (\(N_A\)) of individual electrons.

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The total electrical charge per mole of electrons is: \[F = N_A \times e\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\[F = (6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}) \times (1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}) = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\] In standard practice and approximate calculations, this value is rounded to \(96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\) (approximately \(96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\)).

answer.text: \(96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\) (commonly approximated as \(96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q44 - Calculation of Faradays required for electrolytic deposition of calcium
