इंसुलिन, ग्लूकागॉन, थायरॉक्सिन और एड्रीनल कॉर्टिकोस्टेरॉयड के कार्य और रासायनिक प्रकृति सही बताई गई है, जबकि एपिनेफ्रीन और नॉर-एपिनेफ्रीन को जननग्रंथि स्टेरॉयड के रूप में गलत वर्गीकृत किया गया है। अतः, केवल कथन I, III और IV सही हैं।

answer.text: Statements I, II and III only are correct
Statements II, III and IV only are correct
Statements I, III and IV only are correct
Statements I, II, III and IV are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q01 - Matching vitamins with their deficiency diseases

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Vitamin) List-II (Deficiency Disease)
(A) Vitamin A(I) Beri beri
(B) Vitamin B1(II) Convulsions
(C) Vitamin C(III) Xerophthalmia
(D) Vitamin B6(IV) Scurvy

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Vitamin A deficiency leads to xerophthalmia (hardening of cornea of eye) and night blindness.

Step 2
Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency results in beri beri, characterized by loss of appetite and retarded growth.

Step 3
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency causes scurvy, which is manifested by bleeding gums.

Step 4
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency leads to convulsions.

Final Answer
Vitamin A pairs with Xerophthalmia; Vitamin B1 pairs with Beri beri; Vitamin C pairs with Scurvy; and Vitamin B6 pairs with Convulsions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q02 - Classification and examples of dietary carbohydrates

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Carbohydrate) List-II (Classification / Type)
(A) Glucose(I) Main storage polysaccharide of plants
(B) Sucrose(II) Ketohexose monosaccharide
(C) Fructose(III) Aldohexose monosaccharide
(D) Starch(IV) Disaccharide yielding glucose and fructose

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Glucose is an aldohexose monomer having the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\) with an aldehyde functional group and five hydroxyl groups.

Step 2
Sucrose is a common disaccharide that on hydrolysis gives an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose.

Step 3
Fructose is a natural ketohexose monosaccharide containing a ketonic functional group at carbon-2.

Step 4
Starch is the primary storage polysaccharide of plants, consisting of amylose and amylopectin polymers of \(\alpha\)-glucose.

Final Answer
Glucose pairs with Aldohexose monosaccharide; Sucrose pairs with Disaccharide yielding glucose and fructose; Fructose pairs with Ketohexose monosaccharide; and Starch pairs with Main storage polysaccharide of plants.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q03 - Reactions of glucose and structural deductions

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Reaction of Glucose) List-II (Structural Inference / Product)
(A) Prolonged heating with \(\mathrm{HI}\)(I) Formation of gluconic acid indicating an aldehydic group
(B) Reaction with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water(II) Formation of saccharic acid indicating a primary alcoholic group
(C) Oxidation with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)(III) Formation of pentaacetate indicating five \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups
(D) Reaction with acetic anhydride(IV) Formation of \(n\)-hexane indicating a continuous six-carbon chain

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Heating glucose with hydroiodic acid (\(\mathrm{HI}\)) for a prolonged period yields \(n\)-hexane, which confirms that all six carbon atoms are joined in an unbranched straight chain.

Step 2
Reaction of glucose with a mild oxidising agent such as bromine water oxidises the terminal carbonyl group to a carboxyl group, forming gluconic acid, which confirms that the carbonyl group is an aldehyde.

Step 3
Oxidation of glucose with nitric acid oxidises both the terminal aldehyde and the primary alcohol group to dicarboxylic acid (saccharic acid), proving the presence of a primary alcoholic group.

Step 4
Acetylation of glucose with acetic anhydride gives a stable pentaacetate derivative, confirming that glucose contains five hydroxyl groups attached to distinct carbon atoms.

Final Answer
Prolonged heating with \(\mathrm{HI}\) pairs with Formation of \(n\)-hexane indicating a continuous six-carbon chain; Reaction with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water pairs with Formation of gluconic acid indicating an aldehydic group; Oxidation with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) pairs with Formation of saccharic acid indicating a primary alcoholic group; and Reaction with acetic anhydride pairs with Formation of pentaacetate indicating five \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q04 - Levels of protein organization and denaturation

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Structural Level / Feature) List-II (Description / Key Characteristic)
(A) Primary structure(I) Spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits
(B) Secondary structure(II) Destruction of \(2^\circ\) and \(3^\circ\) structures while \(1^\circ\) remains intact
(C) Quaternary structure(III) Regular folding into \(\alpha\)-helix or \(\beta\)-pleated sheet by hydrogen bonds
(D) Denaturation of protein(IV) Sequence in which specific amino acids are linked in a polypeptide

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Primary structure refers to the exact linear sequence of amino acids covalently linked by peptide bonds along a polypeptide chain.

Step 2
Secondary structure refers to the localized conformation assumed by the polypeptide backbone, predominantly stabilized by intramolecular or intermolecular hydrogen bonds into \(\alpha\)-helices or \(\beta\)-pleated sheets.

Step 3
Quaternary structure describes the geometric and spatial assembly of two or more separate polypeptide subunits relative to one another in oligomeric proteins.

Step 4
Denaturation is the process wherein physical factors (such as temperature) or chemical factors (such as pH change) disrupt hydrogen bonds and tertiary conformations, causing loss of biological activity while leaving the primary covalent peptide backbone intact.

Final Answer
Primary structure pairs with Sequence in which specific amino acids are linked in a polypeptide; Secondary structure pairs with Regular folding into \(\alpha\)-helix or \(\beta\)-pleated sheet by hydrogen bonds; Quaternary structure pairs with Spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits; and Denaturation of protein pairs with Destruction of \(2^\circ\) and \(3^\circ\) structures while \(1^\circ\) remains intact.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q05 - Solubility characteristics and deficiency of vitamins

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Vitamin) List-II (Deficiency Sign / Characteristic)
(A) Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)(I) Increased blood clotting time
(B) Vitamin B12(II) Cheilosis and burning sensation of skin
(C) Vitamin E(III) Pernicious anaemia; water soluble but stored in the body
(D) Vitamin K(IV) Increased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Deficiency of vitamin B2 (riboflavin) causes cheilosis (fissuring at the corners of the mouth and lips), digestive disorders, and a burning sensation of the skin.

Step 2
Vitamin B12 is unique among water-soluble vitamins because it can be stored in the body; its deficiency results in pernicious anaemia (red blood cells deficient in haemoglobin).

Step 3
Deficiency of vitamin E (a fat-soluble antioxidant vitamin) leads to increased fragility of red blood cells and muscular weakness.

Step 4
Vitamin K is essential for blood coagulation; its deficiency results in delayed coagulation and increased blood clotting time.

Final Answer
Vitamin B2 pairs with Cheilosis and burning sensation of skin; Vitamin B12 pairs with Pernicious anaemia; water soluble but stored in the body; Vitamin E pairs with Increased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness; and Vitamin K pairs with Increased blood clotting time.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q06 - Chemical nature and biological functions of hormones

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Hormone) List-II (Nature / Physiological Role)
(A) Insulin(I) Iodinated tyrosine derivative regulating basal metabolism
(B) Thyroxine(II) Polypeptide hormone keeping blood glucose within narrow limits
(C) Glucocorticoids(III) Steroid hormone preparing uterus for implantation of fertilised egg
(D) Progesterone(IV) Adrenal cortical steroids controlling carbohydrate metabolism and stress

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Insulin is a polypeptide hormone produced by the pancreas that lowers elevated blood glucose and maintains it within narrow physiological limits.

Step 2
Thyroxine is an iodinated amino acid derivative synthesized from tyrosine in the thyroid gland; abnormally low levels cause hypothyroidism.

Step 3
Glucocorticoids are steroid hormones produced by the adrenal cortex that regulate carbohydrate metabolism, modulate inflammatory responses, and manage stress.

Step 4
Progesterone is a female steroid sex hormone responsible for preparing and maintaining the uterine lining for implantation of the fertilised egg.

Final Answer
Insulin pairs with Polypeptide hormone keeping blood glucose within narrow limits; Thyroxine pairs with Iodinated tyrosine derivative regulating basal metabolism; Glucocorticoids pairs with Adrenal cortical steroids controlling carbohydrate metabolism and stress; and Progesterone pairs with Steroid hormone preparing uterus for implantation of fertilised egg.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q07 - Components and bonds in nucleic acid architecture

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Component / Entity) List-II (Chemical Definition / Structure)
(A) Nucleoside(I) Linkage joining \(5'\) and \(3'\) carbons of adjacent pentose sugars
(B) Nucleotide(II) Unit formed by attachment of a nitrogenous base to \(1'\)-position of sugar
(C) Phosphodiester bond(III) Base pairing between adenine and thymine, or guanine and cytosine
(D) Complementary base pairing(IV) Unit containing base, pentose sugar, and phosphate at \(5'\)-position

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
A nucleoside is a molecular unit formed exclusively by the attachment of a purine or pyrimidine heterocyclic base to the \(1'\)-carbon of a pentose sugar moiety.

Step 2
A nucleotide is formed when a nucleoside is esterified with phosphoric acid at the \(5'\)-position of the pentose sugar.

Step 3
Phosphodiester linkages connect consecutive nucleotide units between the \(5'\)-hydroxyl of one sugar unit and the \(3'\)-hydroxyl of the adjoining sugar unit to construct polynucleotide chains.

Step 4
Complementary base pairing in double-helical DNA relies on specific hydrogen bonding between adenine and thymine, and between guanine and cytosine.

Final Answer
Nucleoside pairs with Unit formed by attachment of a nitrogenous base to \(1'\)-position of sugar; Nucleotide pairs with Unit containing base, pentose sugar, and phosphate at \(5'\)-position; Phosphodiester bond pairs with Linkage joining \(5'\) and \(3'\) carbons of adjacent pentose sugars; and Complementary base pairing pairs with Base pairing between adenine and thymine, or guanine and cytosine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q08 - Specific glycosidic linkages in carbohydrates

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Carbohydrate) List-II (Constituent Units and Glycosidic Linkage)
(A) Sucrose(I) Linear \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) \(\alpha\)-glucose chain with branching at \(\mathrm{C1-C6}\)
(B) Lactose(II) \(\beta\)-D-Galactose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose linked via \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) glycosidic bond
(C) Cellulose(III) \(\alpha\)-D-Glucose \(\mathrm{C1}\) linked to \(\beta\)-D-fructose \(\mathrm{C2}\)
(D) Amylopectin(IV) Straight chain of \(\beta\)-D-glucose units joined by \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) glycosidic bond

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Sucrose is a non-reducing disaccharide composed of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and \(\beta\)-D-fructose, held together by a glycosidic linkage between \(\mathrm{C1}\) of glucose and \(\mathrm{C2}\) of fructose.

Step 2
Lactose (milk sugar) is a reducing disaccharide composed of \(\beta\)-D-galactose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose linked through a glycosidic bond between \(\mathrm{C1}\) of galactose and \(\mathrm{C4}\) of glucose.

Step 3
Cellulose is an unbranched structural polysaccharide composed exclusively of \(\beta\)-D-glucose residues joined together by \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) glycosidic linkages.

Step 4
Amylopectin is the water-insoluble fraction of starch; it features a linear chain of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose units linked by \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) glycosidic bonds, with branching occurring via \(\mathrm{C1-C6}\) glycosidic linkages.

Final Answer
Sucrose pairs with \(\alpha\)-D-Glucose \(\mathrm{C1}\) linked to \(\beta\)-D-fructose \(\mathrm{C2}\); Lactose pairs with \(\beta\)-D-Galactose and \(\beta\)-D-glucose linked via \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) glycosidic bond; Cellulose pairs with Straight chain of \(\beta\)-D-glucose units joined by \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) glycosidic bond; and Amylopectin pairs with Linear \(\mathrm{C1-C4}\) \(\alpha\)-glucose chain with branching at \(\mathrm{C1-C6}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q09 - Structural characteristics and side chains of amino acids

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Amino Acid) List-II (Side Chain \(-\mathrm{R}\) / Specific Property)
(A) Glycine(I) Side chain \(-\mathrm{CH_2-SH}\); sulfur-containing neutral amino acid
(B) Lysine(II) Side chain \(-\mathrm{H}\); achiral and optically inactive
(C) Glutamic acid(III) Side chain \(-(\mathrm{CH_2})_4-\mathrm{NH_2}\); basic essential amino acid
(D) Cysteine(IV) Side chain \(-\mathrm{CH_2-CH_2-COOH}\); acidic amino acid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Glycine possesses a hydrogen atom as its side chain (\(-\mathrm{R} = -\mathrm{H}\)), making its \(\alpha\)-carbon non-asymmetric; hence, it is the only naturally occurring optically inactive \(\alpha\)-amino acid.

Step 2
Lysine contains a butylamino group in its side chain (\(-(\mathrm{CH_2})_4-\mathrm{NH_2}\)), giving it two amino groups versus one carboxyl group, classifying it as a basic essential amino acid.

Step 3
Glutamic acid contains a second carboxylic acid group in its side chain (\(-\mathrm{CH_2-CH_2-COOH}\)), classifying it as a dicarboxylic acidic amino acid.

Step 4
Cysteine contains a thiol group in its side chain (\(-\mathrm{CH_2-SH}\)), making it a sulfur-bearing neutral amino acid involved in disulphide linkage formation.

Final Answer
Glycine pairs with Side chain \(-\mathrm{H}\); achiral and optically inactive; Lysine pairs with Side chain \(-(\mathrm{CH_2})_4-\mathrm{NH_2}\); basic essential amino acid; Glutamic acid pairs with Side chain \(-\mathrm{CH_2-CH_2-COOH}\); acidic amino acid; and Cysteine pairs with Side chain \(-\mathrm{CH_2-SH}\); sulfur-containing neutral amino acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MATCHING_Q10 - Structural forms and functional attributes of biomolecules

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Biomolecular Term / Entity) List-II (Defining Feature / Chemical Property)
(A) Anomers(I) Lowers activation energy of sucrose hydrolysis to \(2.15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(B) Zwitter ion(II) Equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose with net laevorotation
(C) Invert sugar(III) Diastereomers differing only in configuration at \(\mathrm{C1}\) hemiacetal carbon
(D) Sucrase(IV) Dipolar neutral species demonstrating amphoteric chemical behaviour

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1
Anomers are cyclic hemiacetal isomers (such as \(\alpha\)- and \(\beta\)-D-glucose) that differ in configuration specifically at the carbonyl carbon before cyclisation (the anomeric carbon, \(\mathrm{C1}\)).

Step 2
A zwitter ion is an internal dipolar salt formed by proton transfer from the carboxyl group to the amino group, bearing both positive and negative charges, and displaying amphoteric reactivity.

Step 3
Invert sugar refers to the equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose produced upon sucrose hydrolysis; because the laevorotation of fructose (\(-92.4^\circ\)) exceeds the dextrorotation of glucose (\(+52.5^\circ\)), the net optical rotation inverts from dextro to laevo.

Step 4
Sucrase is an enzyme biocatalyst that reduces the activation energy for the hydrolysis of sucrose from \(6.22\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (for acid hydrolysis) down to \(2.15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Answer
Anomers pairs with Diastereomers differing only in configuration at \(\mathrm{C1}\) hemiacetal carbon; Zwitter ion pairs with Dipolar neutral species demonstrating amphoteric chemical behaviour; Invert sugar pairs with Equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose with net laevorotation; and Sucrase pairs with Lowers activation energy of sucrose hydrolysis to \(2.15\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_NUMERICAL_Q01 - Chiral carbon count in open chain glucose

questiontext.text: Based on the open-chain structural formula of D-(+)-glucose, how many asymmetric (chiral) carbon atoms are present in a single molecule of glucose?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The open-chain structure of D-(+)-glucose is an aldohexose with the molecular formula \( \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6 \) and structural formula \( \mathrm{CHO}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A carbon atom is asymmetric (chiral) if it is bonded to four chemically distinct substituent groups.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Evaluate each of the six carbon atoms in the chain: C-1 through C-6.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Carbon-1 is an aldehyde carbon (\( -\mathrm{CHO} \)), which is \( \mathrm{sp}^2 \)-hybridised and bonded to only three groups (not chiral). Carbon-2 is bonded to \( -\mathrm{H} \), \( -\mathrm{OH} \), \( -\mathrm{CHO} \), and \( -(\mathrm{CHOH})_3-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \) (chiral). Carbon-3 is bonded to \( -\mathrm{H} \), \( -\mathrm{OH} \), \( -\mathrm{CHOH}-\mathrm{CHO} \), and \( -(\mathrm{CHOH})_2-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \) (chiral). Carbon-4 is bonded to \( -\mathrm{H} \), \( -\mathrm{OH} \), \( -(\mathrm{CHOH})_2-\mathrm{CHO} \), and \( -\mathrm{CHOH}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \) (chiral). Carbon-5 is bonded to \( -\mathrm{H} \), \( -\mathrm{OH} \), \( -(\mathrm{CHOH})_3-\mathrm{CHO} \), and \( -\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \) (chiral). Carbon-6 is a primary alcohol carbon (\( -\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)) bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms (achiral). Thus, carbons C-2, C-3, C-4, and C-5 are chiral.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The total count of chiral carbon atoms is 4, which is physically consistent with \( 2^4 = 16 \) possible open-chain stereoisomers. The final numerical value is 4.

Final Answer:
The correct numerical value is 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_NUMERICAL_Q02 - Net specific rotation of invert sugar

questiontext.text: During the hydrolysis of sucrose, an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose is produced. If the specific rotation of D-(+)-glucose is \( +52.5^\circ \) and that of D-(-)-fructose is \( -92.4^\circ \), calculate the net specific optical rotation of the resulting equimolar mixture in degrees.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Specific optical rotation of D-(+)-glucose: \( [\alpha]_D^{\text{glucose}} = +52.5^\circ \). Specific optical rotation of D-(-)-fructose: \( [\alpha]_D^{\text{fructose}} = -92.4^\circ \). Sucrose hydrolyses to yield an equimolar (1:1) mixture of both monosaccharides.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Dextrorotatory values are taken as positive (+) and laevorotatory values are taken as negative (-). Both monosaccharides contribute equally on an equimolar basis in solution.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The net specific optical rotation of an equimolar binary mixture is the arithmetic mean of the specific rotations of the two components: \[ [\alpha]_D^{\text{net}} = \frac{[\alpha]_D^{\text{glucose}} + [\alpha]_D^{\text{fructose}}}{2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given numerical values into the equation: \[ [\alpha]_D^{\text{net}} = \frac{+52.5^\circ + (-92.4^\circ)}{2} \] Calculate the numerator: \[ +52.5 - 92.4 = -39.9^\circ \] Divide by 2: \[ [\alpha]_D^{\text{net}} = \frac{-39.9^\circ}{2} = -19.95^\circ \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The negative sign correctly indicates laevorotation, confirming why the product is termed invert sugar. The final numerical value is -19.95.

Final Answer:
The correct numerical value is -19.95 degrees.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_NUMERICAL_Q03 - Activation energy reduction by sucrase enzyme

questiontext.text: The activation energy for the chemical acid hydrolysis of sucrose is \( 6.22\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \), whereas when hydrolysed biochemically by the enzyme sucrase, the activation energy is \( 2.15\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \). Calculate the magnitude of reduction in activation energy brought about by the enzyme in \( \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Activation energy for acid-catalysed hydrolysis: \( E_{a,\text{acid}} = 6.22\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \). Activation energy for enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis: \( E_{a,\text{enzyme}} = 2.15\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Enzymatic biocatalysis lowers the activation barrier. The magnitude of reduction is a positive quantity defined as the difference between the uncatalysed/acid-catalysed and enzymatically catalysed pathways.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of reduction in activation energy is given by: \[ \Delta E_a = E_{a,\text{acid}} - E_{a,\text{enzyme}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given numerical values: \[ \Delta E_a = 6.22\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} - 2.15\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \] Perform the subtraction: \[ \Delta E_a = 4.07\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The units are \( \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \), and the reduction of 4.07 is physically plausible for biological enzyme efficiency. The final numerical value is 4.07.

Final Answer:
The correct numerical value is 4.07 kJ/mol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_NUMERICAL_Q04 - Theoretical yield of glucose from sucrose

questiontext.text: Calculate the mass in grams of D-glucose produced by the complete acid hydrolysis of \( 342\ \mathrm{g} \) of cane sugar (sucrose, \( \mathrm{C}_{12}\mathrm{H}_{22}\mathrm{O}_{11} \)). (Molar mass of \( \mathrm{C} = 12\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \), \( \mathrm{H} = 1\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \), \( \mathrm{O} = 16\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial mass of sucrose: \( m_{\text{sucrose}} = 342\ \mathrm{g} \). Atomic masses: \( \mathrm{C} = 12\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \), \( \mathrm{H} = 1\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \), \( \mathrm{O} = 16\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \). Complete hydrolysis is assumed.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The reaction goes to 100% completion according to the stoichiometric hydrolysis equation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Stoichiometric chemical equation: \[ \mathrm{C}_{12}\mathrm{H}_{22}\mathrm{O}_{11} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H}^+} \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6\,(\text{glucose}) + \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6\,(\text{fructose}) \] Molar mass formula: \( M = \sum n_i A_i \). Moles: \( n = \frac{m}{M} \). Mass produced: \( m = n \times M \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate molar mass of sucrose (\( \mathrm{C}_{12}\mathrm{H}_{22}\mathrm{O}_{11} \)): \[ M_{\text{sucrose}} = (12 \times 12) + (22 \times 1) + (11 \times 16) = 144 + 22 + 176 = 342\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \] Calculate moles of sucrose: \[ n_{\text{sucrose}} = \frac{342\ \mathrm{g}}{342\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1}} = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol} \] From stoichiometry, 1 mole of sucrose yields 1 mole of D-glucose. Molar mass of D-glucose (\( \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6 \)): \[ M_{\text{glucose}} = (6 \times 12) + (12 \times 1) + (6 \times 16) = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} \] Mass of D-glucose produced: \[ m_{\text{glucose}} = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol} \times 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol}^{-1} = 180\ \mathrm{g} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Conservation of mass check: 342 g sucrose + 18 g water = 360 g total products (180 g glucose + 180 g fructose). The final numerical value is 180.

Final Answer:
The correct numerical value is 180 g.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_NUMERICAL_Q05 - Hydrogen bond calculation in DNA segment

questiontext.text: A synthetic double-stranded DNA segment contains 25 base pairs. If 15 of these base pairs are Adenine-Thymine (A-T) pairs and 10 are Guanine-Cytosine (G-C) pairs, calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds holding the two complementary strands together.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total number of base pairs = 25. Number of Adenine-Thymine (A-T) base pairs = 15. Number of Guanine-Cytosine (G-C) base pairs = 10.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard Watson-Crick base-pairing model applies in the B-DNA double helix.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to the double strand helix structure of DNA, Adenine forms 2 hydrogen bonds with Thymine (\( \mathrm{A}=\mathrm{T} \)), and Guanine forms 3 hydrogen bonds with Cytosine (\( \mathrm{G}\equiv\mathrm{C} \)). Total hydrogen bonds: \[ N_{\mathrm{H\text{-bonds}}} = 2 \times N_{\mathrm{A-T}} + 3 \times N_{\mathrm{G-C}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate hydrogen bonds from A-T base pairs: \[ N_{\mathrm{H, A-T}} = 15 \times 2 = 30 \] Calculate hydrogen bonds from G-C base pairs: \[ N_{\mathrm{H, G-C}} = 10 \times 3 = 30 \] Sum the contributions: \[ N_{\mathrm{total}} = 30 + 30 = 60 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each base pair has between 2 and 3 hydrogen bonds, so for 25 base pairs, total bonds must lie strictly between 50 and 75. 60 satisfies this range. The final numerical value is 60.

Final Answer:
The correct numerical value is 60.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Hierarchical structural levels of protein organization

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following structural levels of protein organization in increasing order of structural complexity, from the fundamental amino acid sequence to the highest multi-subunit assembly:

  1. Primary structure
  2. Quaternary structure
  3. Secondary structure
  4. Tertiary structure

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Proteins are macromolecular polymers organized into four distinct structural hierarchies based on spatial conformation and degree of folding.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structural Levels
The primary structure is the fundamental linear sequence of α-amino acids linked together by covalent peptide bonds. The secondary structure refers to localized regular conformations of the polypeptide chain backbone, primarily α-helices and β-pleated sheets stabilized by intramolecular or intermolecular hydrogen bonds. The tertiary structure represents the comprehensive three-dimensional folding of the entire polypeptide chain into compact fibrous or globular shapes, stabilized by hydrogen bonding, disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions, and ionic attractions. The quaternary structure arises only in multi-subunit proteins and represents the specific spatial arrangement and non-covalent assembly of two or more independent tertiary subunits into a biologically functioning complex.

Step 3: Sequencing by Complexity
Arranging the levels from lowest complexity to highest complexity gives: primary structure, followed by secondary structure, followed by tertiary structure, and finally quaternary structure.

Step 4: Final Answer
The correct sequence in increasing order of structural complexity is Primary structure → Secondary structure → Tertiary structure → Quaternary structure (I → III → IV → II).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Logical steps in glucose structure elucidation

questiontext.text:
Consider the following chemical reactions and analyses used to deduce the open-chain structure of D-glucose:

  1. Heating with hydroiodic acid (\(\mathrm{HI}\)) for a prolonged period to yield \(n\)-hexane, demonstrating a continuous six-carbon unbranched chain.
  2. Elemental analysis and molecular weight determination establishing the molecular formula as \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\).
  3. Reaction with hydroxylamine (\(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\)) to form an oxime, confirming the presence of a carbonyl group.
  4. Oxidation with mild bromine water to yield gluconic acid, indicating that the carbonyl group is an aldehyde.
  5. Oxidation of glucose with concentrated nitric acid (\(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)) to yield the dicarboxylic acid saccharic acid, confirming the presence of a primary alcoholic group.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of structural deduction from basic composition to full functional group assignment?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The structural elucidation of an organic natural product follows a rigorous logical progression: first determining the molecular formula, then establishing the carbon skeleton backbone, identifying general functional groups, and subsequently determining their specific nature and spatial placement.

Step 2: Analysis of Experimental Evidence
First, quantitative elemental composition analysis and colligative property measurements established the molecular formula of glucose as \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\). Second, prolonged heating with \(\mathrm{HI}\) and red phosphorus completely reduced glucose to \(n\)-hexane, proving that all six carbon atoms are linked in an unbranched, straight chain. Third, condensation of glucose with hydroxylamine to form a monoxime, as well as addition of hydrogen cyanide to form a cyanohydrin, confirmed the presence of a carbonyl functionality (\(\mathrm{>C=O}\)). Fourth, mild oxidation with bromine water selectively oxidized the carbonyl group without affecting alcoholic groups to produce the six-carbon monocarboxylic acid gluconic acid, confirming that the carbonyl group is an aldehydic group located at the terminus (C1). Fifth, stronger oxidation with nitric acid oxidised both the terminal aldehyde and the opposite terminal primary alcohol to yield saccharic acid (a dicarboxylic acid), proving that the terminal carbon (C6) is a primary alcohol group (\(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\)).

Step 3: Logical Ordering
The logical order of deduction proceeds from establishing the molecular formula, to verifying the six-carbon continuous chain, identifying the carbonyl group, characterizing the aldehyde group, and finally identifying the primary alcoholic group.

Step 4: Final Answer
The correct logical sequence of structural deduction is II → I → III → IV → V.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Carbohydrates arranged by increasing hydrolysis yield

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four carbohydrates:

  1. Starch
  2. Fructose
  3. Raffinose
  4. Maltose

Which of the following represents the correct sequence when these carbohydrates are arranged in increasing order of the number of monosaccharide units produced upon complete acid hydrolysis of one molecule of each?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbohydrates are classified systematically by their hydrolysis behavior into monosaccharides (cannot be hydrolysed further), oligosaccharides (yield 2 to 10 monosaccharide units), and polysaccharides (yield a very large number of monosaccharide units, typically hundreds to thousands).

Step 2: Hydrolysis Yield of Each Compound
Fructose is a monosaccharide (ketohexose) that cannot undergo further hydrolytic cleavage into simpler polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; thus, one molecule yields exactly 1 monosaccharide unit. Maltose is a disaccharide composed of two α-D-glucose units joined by an α(1→4) glycosidic bond; complete hydrolysis of one molecule yields exactly 2 monosaccharide units of glucose. Raffinose is a trisaccharide found in sugar beets and beans; complete hydrolysis of one molecule yields exactly 3 monosaccharide units (one D-galactose, one D-glucose, and one D-fructose). Starch is a high-molecular-weight polysaccharide composed of repeating amylose and amylopectin glucose polymers; complete hydrolysis of one macromolecule yields hundreds to thousands of D-glucose monosaccharide units.

Step 3: Sequence Determination
Comparing the number of monosaccharide units yielded per molecule: Fructose yields 1 unit, Maltose yields 2 units, Raffinose yields 3 units, and Starch yields many units (>100). Thus, the order of increasing yield is Fructose < Maltose < Raffinose < Starch.

Step 4: Final Answer
The correct sequence in increasing order of monosaccharide units yielded upon complete hydrolysis is II < IV < III < I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Stepwise chemical synthesis of a polynucleotide strand

questiontext.text:
The chemical construction of a polynucleotide strand from fundamental precursor units proceeds through defined stages:

  1. Coupling of a heterocyclic nitrogenous base to the \(1'\)-carbon of a β-D-pentose sugar via an N-glycosidic linkage.
  2. Esterification of the \(5'\)-hydroxyl group of the resulting nucleoside with a phosphate group to produce a nucleotide.
  3. Condensation polymerization forming phosphodiester linkages between the \(3'\)-hydroxyl group of one nucleotide and the \(5'\)-hydroxyl group of an adjacent nucleotide.
  4. Elongation into a macromolecular polynucleotide chain with an alternating sugar-phosphate backbone.

What is the correct sequential order of these stages during the assembly of a polynucleotide chain?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polynucleotides (DNA and RNA) are biopolymers built through hierarchical chemical steps: base-sugar combination to form a nucleoside, phosphorylation to form a nucleotide monomer, and sequential phosphodiester coupling between nucleotides to form the polymeric chain.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Chemical Assembly
In the initial stage, a heterocyclic nitrogenous purine (adenine, guanine) or pyrimidine (cytosine, thymine, uracil) base attaches covalently to the \(1'\)-carbon of β-D-ribose or β-D-2-deoxyribose via an N-glycosidic linkage to yield a nucleoside. In the second stage, the primary alcohol group at position \(5'\) of the sugar moiety undergoes esterification with phosphoric acid to form a nucleotide (nucleoside \(5'\)-phosphate). In the third stage, successive nucleotide monomers are joined together as the \(3'\)-hydroxyl group of the pentose sugar of one nucleotide reacts with the \(5'\)-phosphate group of the succeeding nucleotide, establishing a \(3',5'\)-phosphodiester linkage. In the fourth stage, repeated successive phosphodiester link formations yield an extended polynucleotide chain consisting of a constant sugar-phosphate backbone with nitrogenous bases projecting laterally.

Step 3: Sequential Ordering
The stepwise progression from precursors to polymer is: nucleoside formation via N-glycosidic coupling, nucleotide formation via \(5'\)-esterification, phosphodiester bridge formation between adjacent nucleotides, and elongation into a complete polynucleotide chain.

Step 4: Final Answer
The correct sequential order of stages is I → II → III → IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Mechanistic sequence of events during protein denaturation

questiontext.text:
When a native globular protein is subjected to physical changes such as heating or chemical changes such as alteration of pH, it undergoes denaturation. Arrange the following events occurring during denaturation in their correct sequential order:

  1. Native folded globular protein maintaining its active secondary and tertiary conformation via specific non-covalent interactions.
  2. Disruption of hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and dipole-dipole attractions by thermal kinetic energy or pH-induced charge alterations.
  3. Uncoiling of α-helices and unfolding of β-sheets, with loss of tertiary and secondary structure while covalent peptide bonds remain intact.
  4. Exposure of previously buried hydrophobic non-polar amino acid side chains to the surrounding polar solvent.
  5. Hydrophobic aggregation and cross-linking of exposed polypeptide chains resulting in coagulation and irreversible loss of biological activity.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Denaturation is a progressive conformational breakdown in which a protein loses its higher-order spatial architecture (quaternary, tertiary, and secondary structures) without the cleavage of primary covalent peptide bonds.

Step 2: Sequence of Denaturation Events
The event begins with a native globular protein in its thermodynamically favored, biologically active native state characterized by organized secondary and tertiary folding. When thermal agitation or extreme pH is applied, the weak stabilizing non-covalent forces (hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, and van der Waals attractions) are perturbed and ruptured first because they have much lower bond dissociation energies than covalent amide bonds. The rupture of these stabilizing bonds leads directly to the uncoiling of α-helices and unfolding of β-sheets, destroying the specific three-dimensional globular conformation while leaving the covalent peptide backbone unbroken. Unfolding exposes the non-polar, hydrophobic amino acid side chains that were previously sequestered inside the hydrophobic interior core to the external aqueous environment. Driven by unfavorable entropic interactions with water, these newly exposed hydrophobic surfaces aggregate with adjacent unfolded polypeptide chains, resulting in irreversible coagulation, insoluble precipitate formation, and total loss of biological activity.

Step 3: Chronological Progression
The order of events is: native active folded protein, followed by disruption of non-covalent stabilizing forces, uncoiling and unfolding of higher-order structures, exposure of interior hydrophobic residues, and concluding with hydrophobic aggregation causing coagulation.

Step 4: Final Answer
The correct sequential order of events during denaturation is I → II → III → IV → V.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Mechanism of cyclic hemiacetal pyranose formation in glucose

questiontext.text:
The cyclic hemiacetal structure of D-glucose accounts for chemical properties unexplained by an open-chain structure, such as mutarotation and non-reactivity toward \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\). Arrange the following steps in the mechanistic sequence of D-glucopyranose ring formation and subsequent anomerization:

  1. Conformational rotation of open-chain D-glucose bringing the nucleophilic hydroxyl oxygen at C5 into spatial proximity with the planar carbonyl group at C1.
  2. Intramolecular nucleophilic attack by the lone pair of the C5 hydroxyl oxygen on the electrophilic carbonyl carbon at C1.
  3. Intramolecular proton transfer to the carbonyl oxygen, yielding a stable six-membered cyclic hemiacetal pyranose ring with generation of a new asymmetric center at C1.
  4. Reversible opening and reclosing of the pyranose ring in aqueous solution establishing a dynamic equilibrium between α and β anomers, manifested as mutarotation.

What is the correct sequential order of these stages?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cyclization of D-glucose to form a pyranose ring occurs via an intramolecular nucleophilic addition of an internal alcoholic hydroxyl group to an aldehyde carbonyl, producing a cyclic hemiacetal with a new stereogenic center.

Step 2: Mechanistic Sequence of Cyclization
The open-chain D-glucose molecule first undergoes conformational rotations around carbon-carbon single bonds to adopt a favorable spatial conformation that places the hydroxyl group on C5 directly adjacent to the trigonal planar carbonyl carbon at C1. The electron-rich lone pair on the C5 hydroxyl oxygen then performs an intramolecular nucleophilic attack on the partially positive carbonyl carbon at C1. Concomitant proton transfer to the carbonyl oxygen completes hemiacetal formation, closing the six-membered pyranose ring and converting the achiral C1 carbon into a new chiral stereocenter termed the anomeric carbon. In aqueous solution, this hemiacetal linkage can reversibly open back to the acyclic intermediate and re-close, establishing a dynamic chemical equilibrium between the α-anomer (hydroxyl at C1 trans to \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\)) and the β-anomer (hydroxyl at C1 cis to \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\)), which is observed physically as mutarotation.

Step 3: Logical Progression
The mechanistic sequence begins with conformational proximity alignment, followed by intramolecular nucleophilic attack, ring closure with creation of the anomeric center, and concludes with dynamic anomeric equilibration in aqueous solution.

Step 4: Final Answer
The correct sequential order of stages is I → II → III → IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q01 - Classification and general formula exception of carbohydrates

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds is classified as a carbohydrate even though its molecular formula does not fit the general hydrate formula \( \mathrm{C}_x(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_y \)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition and Formula of Carbohydrates
Historically, carbohydrates were defined as hydrates of carbon fitting the general formula \( \mathrm{C}_x(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_y \).

Step 2: Evaluation of Compounds
Glucose has the molecular formula \( \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6 \), which fits the general formula as \( \mathrm{C}_6(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_6 \). Acetic acid (\( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{O}_2 \) or \( \mathrm{C}_2(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_2 \)) and formaldehyde (\( \mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{O} \)) fit the formula but are not carbohydrates because they lack polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone structures.

Step 3: Exception Identification
Rhamnose has the molecular formula \( \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_5 \). It does not fit the ratio \( \mathrm{C}_x(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_y \), yet it is chemically an optically active polyhydroxy aldehyde and is classified as a carbohydrate.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Rhamnose (\( \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_5 \)) is a carbohydrate that does not fit the general hydrate formula.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q02 - Chemical definition and classification of carbohydrates

questiontext.text: Acetic acid has the molecular formula \( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{O}_2 \), which can be written as \( \mathrm{C}_2(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_2 \). Despite fitting the general formula of hydrates of carbon, it is not classified as a carbohydrate because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Modern Chemical Definition of Carbohydrates
Chemically, carbohydrates are defined as optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or substances that yield such units upon hydrolysis.

Step 2: Functional Group Analysis of Acetic Acid
Acetic acid contains a single carboxyl group (\( -\mathrm{COOH} \)) attached to a methyl group (\( -\mathrm{CH}_3 \)). It lacks multiple hydroxyl groups and possesses neither an aldehydic nor a ketonic carbonyl center.

Step 3: Optical Activity Consideration
Acetic acid has no asymmetric carbon atom and is completely optically inactive. Hence, it fails both structural and stereochemical criteria required to be classified as a carbohydrate.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Acetic acid is excluded from carbohydrates because it is neither an optically active polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone nor yields such units upon hydrolysis.

answer.text: It is completely insoluble in water and forms cyclic hydrogen-bonded dimers.
It readily reduces Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution in warm conditions.
It contains an aldehyde group linked directly to a secondary alcohol group.
It is neither an optically active polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone nor yields such units upon hydrolysis.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q03 - Reducing nature of monosaccharides with Tollens reagent

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes reducing sugars based on their chemical behaviour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Reducing Sugars
Carbohydrates that reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent are classified as reducing sugars.

Step 2: Behaviour of Monosaccharides
All monosaccharides, whether aldoses (containing free \( -\mathrm{CHO} \)) or ketoses (which isomerise to aldoses in alkaline medium via enediol intermediate), possess reducing properties.

Step 3: Evaluation of Other Carbohydrate Classes
Disaccharides with bonded anomeric carbonyl centers (such as sucrose) are non-reducing. Polysaccharides are high-molecular-weight non-sugars and do not exhibit reducing properties.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: All monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, are reducing sugars.

answer.text: Only aldoses are reducing sugars, whereas ketoses fail to reduce Fehling's solution under any condition.
All monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, reduce Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution.
Polysaccharides like starch and cellulose are reducing sugars because of their numerous terminal glucose units.
Disaccharides in which the functional groups of both monosaccharide units are bonded behave as reducing sugars.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q04 - Commercial preparation of glucose from starch

questiontext.text: Commercially, glucose is obtained on a large scale by the hydrolysis of starch under which of the following reaction conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reaction Equation
The industrial hydrolysis of starch or cellulose proceeds as: \[ (\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{10}\mathrm{O}_5)_n + n\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow[393\ \mathrm{K},\ 2\text{--}3\ \mathrm{atm}]{\mathrm{H}^+} n\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6 \]

Step 2: Identification of Reagent and Temperature
The catalyst is dilute mineral acid (dilute \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \)), the specified reaction temperature is \( 393\ \mathrm{K} \), and elevated pressure of \( 2\text{--}3\ \mathrm{atm} \) is applied.

Step 3: Check against Source Conditions
The conditions specified in the textbook for commercial starch hydrolysis are dilute sulfuric acid at \( 393\ \mathrm{K} \) under \( 2\text{--}3\ \mathrm{atm} \).

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Commercial glucose is prepared by boiling starch with dilute sulfuric acid at 393 K under 2 to 3 atm pressure.

answer.text: Heating starch with concentrated \( \mathrm{HCl} \) at room temperature and atmospheric pressure.
Refluxing starch with alcoholic \( \mathrm{KOH} \) at \( 373\ \mathrm{K} \) under reduced pressure.
Boiling starch with dilute \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \) at \( 393\ \mathrm{K} \) under \( 2\text{--}3\ \mathrm{atm} \) pressure.
Treating starch with bromine water at \( 303\ \mathrm{K} \) under neutral conditions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q05 - Hydrolysis products of maltose disaccharide

questiontext.text: Complete acid or enzymatic hydrolysis of one molecule of maltose yields:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Disaccharide Composition
Disaccharides yield two monosaccharide molecules upon hydrolysis, which may be identical or different.

Step 2: Specific Hydrolysis Reaction of Maltose
Maltose is composed of two \( \alpha \)-D-glucose units joined by a \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) glycosidic linkage: \[ \mathrm{C}_{12}\mathrm{H}_{22}\mathrm{O}_{11} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6 \quad (\text{D-glucose}) \]

Step 3: Distinction from Sucrose and Lactose
Sucrose gives glucose and fructose, while lactose gives glucose and galactose. Maltose specifically yields two molecules of glucose.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Hydrolysis of maltose yields two molecules of D-glucose.

answer.text: One molecule of D-glucose and one molecule of D-fructose.
One molecule of D-glucose and one molecule of D-galactose.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q06 - Optical rotation inversion during sucrose hydrolysis

questiontext.text: Hydrolysis of dextrorotatory sucrose yields an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose, known as invert sugar. The hydrolyzed mixture is laevorotatory because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Optical Rotation of Reactant and Products
Sucrose is dextrorotatory with a specific rotation of \( +66.5^\circ \). Upon hydrolysis, it produces equimolar amounts of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose.

Step 2: Comparison of Specific Rotations
The specific rotation of D-(+)-glucose is \( +52.5^\circ \), while the specific rotation of D-(-)-fructose is \( -92.4^\circ \).

Step 3: Net Optical Rotation Calculation
For an equimolar mixture: \[ [\alpha]_{\text{net}} = \frac{+52.5^\circ + (-92.4^\circ)}{2} = -19.95^\circ \] Because the magnitude of laevorotation of fructose is greater than the dextrorotation of glucose, the overall mixture is laevorotatory.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The hydrolyzed mixture is laevorotatory because the laevorotation of D-(-)-fructose (-92.4 degrees) is greater than the dextrorotation of D-(+)-glucose (+52.5 degrees).

answer.text: D-(+)-glucose undergoes complete mutarotation into an optically inactive racemic mixture.
The laevorotation of D-(-)-fructose (\( -92.4^\circ \)) exceeds the dextrorotation of D-(+)-glucose (\( +52.5^\circ \)).
D-(+)-glucose isomerises completely into D-(-)-fructose under acidic hydrolysis conditions.
The glycosidic oxygen retains a net laevorotatory magnetic dipole moment in solution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q07 - Monomer units and glycosidic linkage in lactose

questiontext.text: Lactose, the disaccharide found in milk, is composed of which monosaccharide units linked by which glycosidic bond?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Constituent Monosaccharides
Lactose (milk sugar) is a disaccharide composed of \( \beta \)-D-galactose and \( \beta \)-D-glucose.

Step 2: Glycosidic Linkage Position
The linkage is formed between carbon-1 (\( \mathrm{C}_1 \)) of \( \beta \)-D-galactose and carbon-4 (\( \mathrm{C}_4 \)) of \( \beta \)-D-glucose.

Step 3: Reducing Property Relation
Because carbon-1 of the glucose unit has a free potential aldehyde group in solution, lactose behaves as a reducing sugar.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Lactose is composed of beta-D-galactose and beta-D-glucose held together by a C1-C4 glycosidic linkage.

answer.text: \( \alpha \)-D-glucose and \( \beta \)-D-fructose joined by a \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_2 \) glycosidic linkage.
Two \( \alpha \)-D-glucose units joined by a \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) glycosidic linkage.
\( \beta \)-D-galactose and \( \beta \)-D-glucose joined by a \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) glycosidic linkage.
\( \beta \)-D-glucose and \( \alpha \)-D-mannose joined by a \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_6 \) glycosidic linkage.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q08 - Comparison of amylose and amylopectin in starch

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly differentiates between the two components of starch, amylose and amylopectin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Amylose Properties
Amylose is the water-soluble fraction comprising about 15–20% of starch. It consists of a long, unbranched chain of 200–1000 \( \alpha \)-D-(+)-glucose units joined by \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) glycosidic linkages.

Step 2: Amylopectin Properties
Amylopectin is the water-insoluble fraction constituting 80–85% of starch. It is a highly branched chain polymer with \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) linkages in the linear chain and \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_6 \) linkages at branching points.

Step 3: Synthesis of Differences
Amylose is water-soluble, unbranched, and represents 15–20%, while amylopectin is water-insoluble, branched, and represents 80–85%.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Amylose is water-soluble (15-20%) and unbranched, while amylopectin is water-insoluble (80-85%) and branched.

answer.text: Amylose is water-insoluble (constituting 80–85% of starch), whereas amylopectin is water-soluble (15–20%) and unbranched.
Both amylose and amylopectin are water-soluble polymers of \( \beta \)-D-glucose units.
Amylose contains branching via \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_6 \) linkages, whereas amylopectin is a strictly linear unbranched chain.
Amylose is water-soluble (constituting 15–20% of starch) and unbranched, whereas amylopectin is water-insoluble (80–85%) and branched.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q09 - Chemical structure and glycosidic linkage of cellulose

questiontext.text: Cellulose, the primary structural component of plant cell walls, is chemically composed of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Monomeric Unit of Cellulose
Cellulose is composed entirely of \( \beta \)-D-glucose units.

Step 2: Chain Architecture and Linkage
The \( \beta \)-D-glucose units are linked in a straight, unbranched chain by glycosidic bonds between carbon-1 of one glucose unit and carbon-4 of the adjacent glucose unit (\( \beta \)-1,4-glycosidic linkage).

Step 3: Structural Significance
Unlike starch (composed of \( \alpha \)-glucose), the \( \beta \)-configuration allows chains to pack tightly into rigid fibrous structures.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Cellulose is a straight-chain polysaccharide composed exclusively of beta-D-glucose units linked by C1-C4 glycosidic bonds.

answer.text: A branched polymer of \( \alpha \)-D-glucose units with \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) and \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_6 \) linkages.
A linear polymer of \( \alpha \)-D-glucose units joined exclusively by \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) glycosidic linkages.
A straight-chain polysaccharide composed exclusively of \( \beta \)-D-glucose units joined by \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) glycosidic linkages.
A mixed polysaccharide containing equimolar \( \alpha \)-D-glucose and \( \beta \)-D-galactose units.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q10 - Structure and comparison of glycogen with amylopectin

questiontext.text: Glycogen, the carbohydrate storage molecule in animals, is often called 'animal starch' because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Storage Role of Glycogen
In animals, carbohydrates are stored primarily in the liver, muscles, and brain in the form of glycogen.

Step 2: Structural Comparison with Starch Components
Glycogen is a polymer of \( \alpha \)-D-glucose with \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_4 \) chains and \( \mathrm{C}_1\text{--}\mathrm{C}_6 \) branches, directly analogous to amylopectin.

Step 3: Distinguishing Feature
The key distinction is that glycogen is even more highly branched than amylopectin, facilitating rapid enzymatic breakdown when the body requires glucose.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Glycogen resembles amylopectin in structure but possesses a higher degree of branching.

answer.text: Its structure consists of unbranched chains identical to amylose.
Its structure is similar to amylopectin, but it is rather more highly branched.
It is composed of \( \beta \)-D-glucose units identical to cellulose.
It is a non-reducing disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q11 - Prolonged heating of glucose with hydroiodic acid

questiontext.text: On prolonged heating with hydroiodic acid (\( \mathrm{HI} \)), D-glucose is converted into which organic compound, confirming that all six carbon atoms are linked in a straight chain?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reaction with HI
Hydroiodic acid in the presence of heat is a strong reducing agent that reduces all carbonyl and hydroxyl groups in polyhydroxy compounds to hydrocarbons.

Step 2: Equation
\[ \mathrm{CHO}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI},\,\Delta} \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3 \quad (n\text{-hexane}) \]

Step 3: Structural Deduction
The formation of \( n \)-hexane demonstrates that the six carbon atoms of glucose form an unbranched, continuous carbon skeleton.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Heating glucose with HI yields n-hexane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q12 - Mild oxidation of glucose with bromine water

questiontext.text: D-Glucose gets oxidised to a six-carbon monocarboxylic acid (gluconic acid) upon reaction with bromine water. This observation confirms:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nature of Bromine Water
Bromine water (\( \mathrm{Br}_2/\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \)) is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes to carboxylic acids but does not oxidise ketones or primary/secondary alcohols under these conditions.

Step 2: Product Formed
Glucose is selectively oxidised to gluconic acid: \[ \mathrm{CHO}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br}_2\ \text{water}} \mathrm{COOH}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \]

Step 3: Conclusion
Because the carbonyl group undergoes mild oxidation to a single carboxyl group without cleavage or oxidation of alcohols, the carbonyl group must be an aldehyde (\( -\mathrm{CHO} \)).

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Oxidation by bromine water to gluconic acid confirms the presence of an aldehydic group.

answer.text: The presence of a ketonic group at carbon-2.
The presence of a primary alcoholic group (\( -\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)).
The presence of an aldehydic group (\( -\mathrm{CHO} \)) in glucose.
The existence of a cyclic hemiacetal pyranose ring.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q13 - Acetylation of glucose confirming five hydroxyl groups

questiontext.text: Acetylation of D-glucose with acetic anhydride produces glucose pentaacetate. The stability of this compound demonstrates that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Acetylation Reaction
Each hydroxyl group reacts with acetic anhydride to form an ester (acetate): \[ \mathrm{CHO}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} + 5\,\mathrm{Ac}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{CHO}-(\mathrm{CHOAc})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OAc} + 5\,\mathrm{AcOH} \]

Step 2: Stoichiometric Evidence
Formation of a pentaacetate proves the presence of exactly five hydroxyl (\( -\mathrm{OH} \)) groups.

Step 3: Chemical Stability Deduction
Compounds having two or more hydroxyl groups on the same carbon atom are generally unstable and eliminate water to form carbonyls. Because glucose pentaacetate is stable, the five hydroxyl groups must reside on five distinct carbon atoms.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The formation of stable glucose pentaacetate confirms five hydroxyl groups attached to five different carbon atoms.

answer.text: All five hydroxyl groups are attached to the same terminal carbon atom.
Five hydroxyl groups are present, and each is attached to a different carbon atom.
Glucose contains a quaternary carbon atom bonded to five acetate groups.
Glucose lacks a carbonyl group in its open-chain structure.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q14 - Stereochemical D-configuration assignment of glucose

questiontext.text: In the standard nomenclature D-(+)-glucose, the letter 'D' signifies that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Significance of D and L Notations
The letters 'D' and 'L' represent relative stereochemical configurations relative to glyceraldehyde, and do not indicate optical rotation.

Step 2: Comparison with Glyceraldehyde
In D-(+)-glyceraldehyde, the \( -\mathrm{OH} \) group on the asymmetric carbon lies on the right-hand side in the Fischer projection.

Step 3: Assignment in Glucose
For monosaccharides, the configuration is assigned based on the lowest asymmetric carbon atom. In glucose, this is C-5. Because the \( -\mathrm{OH} \) at C-5 is on the right, glucose belongs to the D-series. The (+) sign separately denotes that it is dextrorotatory.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The letter 'D' denotes that the hydroxyl group at the lowest asymmetric carbon (C-5) is on the right-hand side.

answer.text: The aqueous solution of glucose rotates the plane of polarised light to the right (dextrorotatory).
All four asymmetric carbon atoms in glucose have their hydroxyl groups oriented to the right.
The hydroxyl group on the lowest asymmetric carbon atom (C-5) lies on the right side in the Fischer projection, matching D-(+)-glyceraldehyde.
The aldehyde group is located on the D-side (dorsal side) of the carbon chain.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q15 - Nitric acid oxidation of glucose to saccharic acid

questiontext.text: When D-glucose is oxidised with concentrated nitric acid, it yields a dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid. Gluconic acid also yields saccharic acid on oxidation with nitric acid. These two observations collectively confirm:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Oxidation Action of Nitric Acid
Nitric acid (\( \mathrm{HNO}_3 \)) is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises both terminal aldehydic groups (\( -\mathrm{CHO} \)) and primary alcoholic groups (\( -\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)) to carboxyl groups (\( -\mathrm{COOH} \)).

Step 2: Reaction with Glucose and Gluconic Acid
Glucose (\( \mathrm{CHO}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)) is converted to saccharic acid (\( \mathrm{COOH}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{COOH} \)). Gluconic acid (\( \mathrm{COOH}-(\mathrm{CHOH})_4-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)), which already has a carboxyl group at C-1, also yields saccharic acid upon \( \mathrm{HNO}_3 \) oxidation.

Step 3: Deduction
Since the \( -\mathrm{CHO} \) at C-1 is already accounted for, the oxidation of the other terminal group to \( -\mathrm{COOH} \) in both glucose and gluconic acid specifically proves that the remaining terminal carbon is a primary alcohol (\( -\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)).

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The formation of saccharic acid from both glucose and gluconic acid confirms the presence of a primary alcoholic group.

answer.text: The presence of a ketonic group at carbon-3 in glucose.
The presence of a primary alcoholic group (\( -\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH} \)) in glucose.
The presence of two aldehydic groups in the open-chain form of glucose.
The absence of secondary alcoholic groups in glucose.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q16 - Stereochemical configuration of naturally occurring alpha amino acids

questiontext.text: Most naturally occurring \( \alpha \)-amino acids obtained from the hydrolysis of proteins possess which stereochemical configuration?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Asymmetry in Amino Acids
Except glycine, all natural \( \alpha \)-amino acids have an asymmetric \( \alpha \)-carbon and exist as stereoisomers.

Step 2: Natural Configuration
Most naturally occurring \( \alpha \)-amino acids belong to the L-series.

Step 3: Fischer Representation
In the standard Fischer projection with the carboxyl group (\( -\mathrm{COOH} \)) at the top and side chain (\( \mathrm{R} \)) at the bottom, L-amino acids have the amino group (\( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \)) positioned on the left-hand side.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Naturally occurring amino acids predominantly have the L-configuration with the amino group on the left.

answer.text: D-Configuration, with the \( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \) group written on the right in the Fischer projection.
L-Configuration, with the \( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \) group written on the left in the Fischer projection.
Racemic mixture with zero net optical activity.
Meso configuration due to an internal plane of symmetry.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q17 - Classification of acidic, basic and neutral amino acids

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs contains amino acids that are both classified as basic amino acids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification Principle
Amino acids are classified as neutral (equal numbers of amino and carboxyl groups), acidic (more carboxyl than amino groups), or basic (more amino groups than carboxyl groups).

Step 2: Evaluation of Options
Aspartic acid and glutamic acid possess two \( -\mathrm{COOH} \) groups and one \( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \) group, making them acidic. Alanine, valine, glycine, and leucine have one \( -\mathrm{COOH} \) and one \( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \), making them neutral.

Step 3: Basic Amino Acids
Lysine contains an extra amino group in its side chain (\( -(\mathrm{CH}_2)_4-\mathrm{NH}_2 \)) and arginine contains a guanidino group, making both of them basic amino acids.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Lysine and arginine are basic amino acids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q18 - Zwitterionic structure and amphoteric property of amino acids

questiontext.text: In aqueous solution, the neutral form of an amino acid undergoes internal proton transfer to form a dipolar ion known as a zwitterion. In this form, the amino acid exhibits amphoteric behaviour because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formation of Zwitterion
In aqueous medium, the acidic carboxyl group loses a proton to form \( -\mathrm{COO}^- \), and the basic amino group accepts a proton to form \( -\mathrm{NH}_3^+ \), creating the dipolar zwitterion \( \mathrm{R}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{NH}_3^+)-\mathrm{COO}^- \).

Step 2: Reaction with Acid
When treated with acid (\( \mathrm{H}^+ \)), the \( -\mathrm{COO}^- \) group accepts a proton to form \( -\mathrm{COOH} \), acting as a base.

Step 3: Reaction with Base
When treated with base (\( \mathrm{OH}^- \)), the \( -\mathrm{NH}_3^+ \) group donates a proton to form \( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \), acting as an acid. Thus, it reacts with both acids and bases, showing amphoteric behaviour.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The zwitterion is amphoteric because the carboxylate group accepts protons from acids and the ammonium group donates protons to bases.

answer.text: Both functional groups lose protons simultaneously in any acidic medium.
It acts exclusively as a strong Lewis acid by accepting electron pairs at the nitrogen atom.
The zwitterion carries an overall positive charge that repels basic reagents.
The carboxylate group (\( -\mathrm{COO}^- \)) can accept a proton from acids, while the ammonium group (\( -\mathrm{NH}_3^+ \)) can donate a proton to bases.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q19 - Optical inactivity of glycine among alpha amino acids

questiontext.text: Which of the following naturally occurring \( \alpha \)-amino acids is optically inactive?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Condition for Optical Activity
A molecule is optically active if it possesses a chiral (asymmetric) carbon atom with four different substituent groups attached to it.

Step 2: Structure of Glycine
The side chain (\( \mathrm{R} \)) in glycine is a hydrogen atom (\( \mathrm{H} \)). Its structural formula is \( \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{COOH} \).

Step 3: Achirality
Because the \( \alpha \)-carbon is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms, it is achiral (not asymmetric). Therefore, glycine is optically inactive, whereas all other natural \( \alpha \)-amino acids are optically active.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Glycine is the only naturally occurring alpha-amino acid that is optically inactive.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q20 - Formation of glycylalanine dipeptide and peptide bond

questiontext.text: When the carboxyl group of glycine combines with the amino group of alanine with the elimination of a water molecule, the resulting product is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Peptide Bond
A peptide bond is an amide linkage (\( -\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}- \)) formed between the \( -\mathrm{COOH} \) group of one amino acid and the \( -\mathrm{NH}_2 \) group of another with loss of water.

Step 2: Reaction Scheme
\[ \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{COOH} \xrightarrow{-\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{COOH} \]

Step 3: Nomenclature of the Dipeptide
Because glycine provides the carboxyl carbon and alanine provides the amino nitrogen, the product is glycylalanine (Gly-Ala).

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The product is the dipeptide glycylalanine (Gly-Ala) containing a peptide linkage.

answer.text: The dipeptide alanylglycine (Ala-Gly), containing an ester linkage.
A polypeptide of high molecular mass with cross-linked disulphide bonds.
A cyclic diamide without any free terminal amino or carboxyl groups.
The dipeptide glycylalanine (Gly-Ala), containing a \( -\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}- \) peptide linkage.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q21 - Classification of proteins into fibrous and globular types

questiontext.text: Proteins can be classified into fibrous and globular proteins on the basis of their molecular shape. Which of the following sets correctly pairs examples of fibrous and globular proteins, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fibrous Proteins
Fibrous proteins consist of parallel polypeptide chains held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, forming insoluble fibre-like structures. Classic examples are keratin (in hair, wool, silk) and myosin (in muscles).

Step 2: Globular Proteins
Globular proteins result when polypeptide chains coil around to produce a spherical shape; they are usually soluble in water. Examples include insulin and albumins.

Step 3: Pairing Check
Keratin and myosin are fibrous, while insulin and albumins are globular.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Keratin and myosin are fibrous proteins, while insulin and albumins are globular proteins.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q22 - Limitations of open-chain structure of glucose

questiontext.text: Which of the following experimental facts could NOT be explained by the open-chain pentahydroxy aldehyde structure of D-glucose?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reactions Explained by Open Chain
Reactions with hydroxylamine, hydrogen cyanide, and bromine water are fully consistent with the presence of a carbonyl/aldehyde group in an open-chain structure.

Step 2: Anomalous Non-Reactions
Despite having an aldehyde group, glucose fails to give Schiff's test, fails to form an addition product with sodium hydrogensulphite (\( \mathrm{NaHSO}_3 \)), and its pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine.

Step 3: Explanation by Cyclic Structure
These anomalies could not be accounted for by the open-chain structure and led to the discovery that glucose exists predominantly as cyclic hemiacetal pyranose anomers in which the aldehyde group is involved in ring formation.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The failure of glucose to give Schiff's test and form a hydrogensulphite addition compound could not be explained by the open-chain structure.

answer.text: Glucose forms an oxime upon treatment with hydroxylamine.
Glucose adds a molecule of hydrogen cyanide to give a cyanohydrin.
Glucose is oxidised by bromine water to form gluconic acid.
Glucose does not give Schiff's test and does not form a hydrogensulphite addition product with \( \mathrm{NaHSO}_3 \).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q23 - Anomeric carbon and cyclic hemiacetal forms of D-glucose

questiontext.text: The two crystalline forms of glucose, \( \alpha \)-D-(+)-glucose and \( \beta \)-D-(+)-glucose, are related to each other as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formation of Cyclic Hemiacetal
When glucose cyclises, the \( -\mathrm{OH} \) group at C-5 adds to the carbonyl group at C-1, generating a new asymmetric center at C-1.

Step 2: Definition of Anomers
Diastereomers of cyclic carbohydrates that differ in configuration specifically at the hemiacetal or hemiketal carbon (C-1 in aldoses) are called anomers, and this carbon is known as the anomeric carbon.

Step 3: Alpha and Beta Forms
In \( \alpha \)-D-glucopyranose, the anomeric \( -\mathrm{OH} \) at C-1 is oriented downwards (on the right in Fischer), whereas in \( \beta \)-D-glucopyranose it is oriented upwards (on the left in Fischer). They are anomers.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The alpha and beta forms of D-glucose are anomers differing only at C-1.

answer.text: Enantiomers, because they are non-superimposable mirror images of each other at every stereocenter.
Anomers, because they differ only in the stereochemical configuration of the hydroxyl group at C-1 (the anomeric carbon).
Constitutional isomers, because they possess completely different molecular formulas and functional groups.
Geometrical isomers, because they arise from restricted rotation around a carbon-carbon double bond.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q24 - Forces stabilizing secondary and tertiary protein structures

questiontext.text: The secondary structure of proteins, including the \( \alpha \)-helix and \( \beta \)-pleated sheet, is primarily stabilized by which type of interaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Secondary Structure
Secondary structure refers to the conformation adopted by the polypeptide backbone due to regular, repetitive folding.

Step 2: Interactions Involved
The secondary structures (both \( \alpha \)-helix and \( \beta \)-pleated sheet) arise due to regular hydrogen bonding between the carbonyl oxygen (\( >\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O} \)) and the amide proton (\( -\mathrm{NH}- \)) of peptide bonds.

Step 3: Distinction from Tertiary Structure
Disulphide linkages, hydrophobic forces, and electrostatic salt bridges mainly contribute to the overall tertiary and quaternary folding.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Secondary protein structures are stabilized by hydrogen bonding between carbonyl and amide groups of peptide linkages.

answer.text: Covalent disulphide cross-links formed between adjacent methionine residues.
Hydrogen bonding between the \( >\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O} \) and \( -\mathrm{NH}- \) groups of the peptide backbone.
Coordinate covalent bonds formed between amide nitrogen atoms and metal ions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q25 - Cyclic furanose structure of D-fructose

questiontext.text: In D-(-)-fructose, the cyclic hemiacetal/hemiketal ring is a five-membered furanose ring. This ring is formed by the intramolecular addition of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fructose Structure
Fructose is a ketohexose with a ketonic carbonyl group located at carbon-2 (\( \mathrm{C}_2 \)).

Step 2: Intramolecular Cyclisation
During cyclisation, the hydroxyl group (\( -\mathrm{OH} \)) attached to carbon-5 (\( \mathrm{C}_5 \)) adds to the ketonic carbonyl at \( \mathrm{C}_2 \).

Step 3: Ring Size and Analogy
This creates a five-membered ring containing four carbon atoms (C-2, C-3, C-4, C-5) and one oxygen atom. By analogy to furan, this ring is called a furanose ring.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The cyclic furanose ring of fructose is formed by the addition of the C-5 hydroxyl group to the C-2 carbonyl group.

answer.text: The hydroxyl group at C-6 to the carbonyl group at C-1.
The hydroxyl group at C-4 to the carbonyl group at C-1.
The hydroxyl group at C-5 to the carbonyl group at C-2.
The hydroxyl group at C-3 to the carbonyl group at C-2.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q26 - Quaternary structure of haemoglobin protein

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the quaternary structure of the transport protein haemoglobin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Quaternary Structure
Proteins composed of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) display quaternary structure, referring to the spatial arrangement of these subunits relative to one another.

Step 2: Haemoglobin Composition
Haemoglobin consists of four individual polypeptide subunits: two \( \alpha \)-subunits and two \( \beta \)-subunits.

Step 3: Architecture
Each subunit has its own tertiary structure, and they assemble cooperatively to form the quaternary tetramer capable of oxygen transport.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: Haemoglobin consists of four subunits (two alpha and two beta chains) in a specific spatial arrangement.

answer.text: It is a single continuous polypeptide chain folded into four identical spherical domains.
It consists of two identical \( \beta \)-pleated sheets held together solely by disulphide bridges.
It is composed of four polypeptide subunits (two \( \alpha \)-type and two \( \beta \)-type chains) arranged in a specific spatial orientation.
It contains four iron atoms linked directly by peptide bonds without any protein subunits.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q27 - Coagulation of egg white as protein denaturation

questiontext.text: The coagulation of egg white upon boiling is a common daily-life manifestation of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Native State Disturbance
When native protein (albumin in egg white) is heated, the thermal agitation disrupts hydrogen bonds and other stabilizing interactions.

Step 2: Unfolding Mechanism
The globules unfold and helical portions uncoil, causing the protein to aggregate and lose its biological solubility and activity.

Step 3: Integrity of Primary Structure
During denaturation, the secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed, but the covalent primary structure (the amino acid sequence) remains intact.

Final Conclusion:
Therefore, the correct answer is: The coagulation of egg white is due to denaturation of proteins where secondary and tertiary structures unfold while primary structure remains intact.

answer.text: Complete enzymatic hydrolysis of peptide bonds into individual free amino acids.
Oxidative cleavage of peptide linkages to yield short-chain carboxylic acids.
Denaturation of proteins, in which secondary and tertiary structures unfold while the primary structure remains intact.
Condensation of amino acid side chains into a covalent polysaccharide network.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q28 - Enzyme activation energy reduction in sucrose hydrolysis

questiontext.text: Enzymes accelerate biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy. For the hydrolysis of sucrose, the activation energy for chemical acid hydrolysis is \( 6.22\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \), whereas when hydrolysed by the enzyme sucrase, it is reduced to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Catalytic Mechanism of Enzymes
Enzymes act as biological catalysts by lowering the activation energy (\( E_a \)) barrier of the reaction pathway.

Step 2: Textbook Benchmark Value
For the hydrolysis of sucrose: \[ \text{Acid hydrolysis: } E_a = 6.22\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \] \[ \text{Sucrase hydrolysis: } E_a = 2.15\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol}^{-1} \]

Step 3: Significance
